metadata.title: 4 Middleman Models in Government Contracting | Which Triggers DOJ Scrutiny?
metadata.author: Squared Compass
metadata.shortDescription:
This video breaks down the complexities of being a government contracting middleman, distinguishing between legitimate and risky approaches. We explore how smart prime contracting and teaming can add value and profit, while cautioning against illegal pass-through or fronting schemes. Understanding these nuances is crucial for small business owners in government contracts to avoid legal pitfalls and ensure proper risk management.

Middleman strategy in government contracting and federal contracting is not automatically bad. In fact, prime contractor teaming is often normal and valuable. The risk starts when a “middleman” turns into a pass-through prime or a set-aside front, especially when the prime adds little value or misrepresents who performs the primary and vital work.

In this video, I break down the 4 middleman models in GovCon and the line between legal teaming and the kind of setup that can trigger SBA ineligibility, bid protests, audits, and in serious cases Department of Justice (DOJ) scrutiny.

✅ In this video you’ll learn:

What “middleman strategy” means in government contracting

The 4 middleman models:

Integrator Prime (value-added prime that manages and integrates subs)

VAR / Distributor (product sourcing plus logistics, warranty, integration, support)

Pass-through Prime (heavy subcontracting with little added value)

Set-aside “Front” (high-risk: paper prime, someone else runs the work)

The 3-question test to evaluate your structure:

What value do we add that benefits the Government?

Is profit applied to prime work or blanket markup on subcontract labor?

For set-asides, are we performing primary and vital work and meeting self-performance limits?

📌 This is Part 1 of our 3-part Middleman Strategy series

Part 1: The 4 models and where the line is

Part 2: Real-world red flags and case patterns that trigger protests, audits, and enforcement attention

Part 3: The compliance playbook: how to structure, price, and describe your value in proposals

💬 Comment below: Which model are you using or seeing most? 1, 2, 3, or 4 (and your niche: IT, construction, services, products).



⚠️ Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and is not legal advice.

#GovernmentContracting #FederalContracting #GovCon #GovernmentContracts #PrimeContractor #Subcontracting #SmallBusiness #SBA #SetAside #Teaming #FAR #Compliance #BidProtest
keywords: how to bid on government contracts

segments.text: ﻿If you are in government contracting or federal contracting, you have heard “middleman strategy.”
Some people say it like it’s a business plan. Some say it like it’s a felony.
Here’s the truth. Middleman can mean smart prime contracting and teaming. Or it can mean
pass-through. Or it can mean set-aside fronting. And if you do the last two wrong, you are not
just risking a bad CPARS. In the worst cases you are risking a date with the Department
of Justice, and yes, that can mean court. Stay with me. In eight minutes you will know
the four middleman models and the three-question test that tells you if your setup is clean, risky,
or one subpoena away from ruining your week. Let’s define this without the legal fog.
In government contracting, “middleman” usually means the prime contractor sits between the
Government and the companies doing most of the hands-on delivery as subcontractors.
And here is the part people forget while arguing about markup. The Government holds
the prime fully responsible for performance, even if subcontractors do most of the work.
So being in the middle is not automatically shady. Sometimes it is literally the job.
Now let’s break the word “middleman” into four
models, because this is where the confusion, and the risk, starts.
Think of it like four lanes on the same highway. Two lanes are normal. One lane gets uncomfortable
questions. One lane gets investigators. Model one is the Integrator Prime.
This is the prime that wins the contract, manages multiple subcontractors, integrates delivery,
owns quality, owns the schedule, and stays accountable to the Government.
You are not just in the middle. You are the quarterback. You call plays and you
take the hit if something goes wrong. Model two is the VAR or Distributor.
This is common in IT and product buys. You source OEM products and add real value through ordering,
logistics, warranty support, integration, and coordination.
If you are reducing lead times, managing deliveries, handling warranty issues,
and making the solution actually work for the agency, that is tangible value.
Model three is the Pass-through Prime. This is where things start to get spicy.
The prime subcontracts almost everything and mostly adds markup. Sometimes there
is a legitimate reason. But if your contribution is basically forwarding
invoices and collecting a percentage, you are drifting into pass-through territory.
That is where the Government starts asking a simple question. Are we paying for value,
or are we paying for air? Model four is the Set-aside Front.
This is the high-risk one. A small business prime is used mainly to
access a set-aside contract while another company performs the primary and vital work.
That can trigger SBA affiliation and ineligibility. And if someone
knowingly misrepresents who actually controls and performs the work,
that is where you start seeing Department of Justice investigations, False Claims Act cases,
and people explaining themselves in court. Quick gut check. Which one do you see the most
in the wild? Model one, two, three, or four. Now let’s talk about how this actually plays
out in real life, because the org chart always looks cleaner than the contract.
Here is the usual sequence. You get positioned on the right
vehicle. Maybe an IDIQ, a GWAC, a Schedule, a BPA, or you chase a standalone award.
You build your team. Subcontractors, teaming agreements, maybe a joint venture.
You propose a solution that includes those subcontractors and you price in
prime management plus subcontract performance. Then you win, and the prime does the unglamorous
work that keeps the contract alive. Managing subcontractors.
Compliance. Deliverables. Invoicing. Changes. Risk management. Quality.
The Government wants one accountable party. Not a group project where everyone
is waiting on someone else. So why do companies use the
middleman strategy at all? Because when it is done right,
it solves real problems. Speed. You can enter a new
agency or vehicle faster by teaming. Capability coverage. You can combine
specialists under one prime. Scalability. You can flex niche
talent without hiring an entire department. And risk control. A real prime coordinates
delivery and quality across multiple sources. Also, let’s be honest. Hiring ten
unicorn experts in thirty days is not a staffing strategy. It is a fantasy novel.
Now we get to the part that actually matters. The Government is not allergic to subcontracting.
The Government is allergic to paying profit for no value.
So here is the line. Are you value-added, or are you a toll booth?
A value-added prime performs subcontract management functions that actually benefit
the Government. Integration across
multiple subcontractors. Quality assurance and acceptance processes. Owning the master schedule.
Coordinating deliveries. Reducing lead times. Managing logistics and warranty issues.
Here is a quick comparison. Scenario one. You coordinate five
subcontractors. You own the schedule. You run QA. You manage risk. You deliver one integrated
solution to the agency. That is value.
Scenario two. Your company logo appears on the invoice, you forward emails between the
Government and the subcontractor, and you take a percentage because you “own the contract.”
That is not value. That is a toll booth. And the Government does not like toll booths.
Especially toll booths charging profit on someone else’s labor.
Now let’s talk about set-asides for a moment, because the guardrails get tighter fast.
If you are in a set-aside contract, two danger zones appear.
First, self-performance limits, also called limitations on subcontracting.
You cannot win a set-aside and hand the majority of the work to a non-qualifying subcontractor.
Second, the SBA looks closely at whether a subcontractor performs the primary and
vital work or whether the prime is unusually reliant on them.
Here is the simple gut check. If the subcontractor provides all
the key personnel, owns the past performance, writes the proposal,
runs the delivery, and you mostly handle billing, that is not a partnership.
That is the kind of fact pattern that leads to size protests, contract terminations,
and in serious situations, Department of Justice scrutiny for misrepresentation.
Alright. I promised you a three-question test you can use in your capture meetings. Here it is.
Question one. What value do we add that
the Government actually benefits from? Integration, QA, schedule ownership,
multi-vendor coordination, logistics, warranty management. Something real.
Question two. Where is our profit applied?
Is it applied to the prime management work we actually perform, or is it just a
blanket percentage applied to subcontract labor?
Healthy primes earn profit on prime work. Toll booths earn profit on other people’s work.
Question three. If this is a set-aside,
are we performing the primary and vital work and meeting the self-performance limits?
Who controls key personnel decisions? Who manages performance? Who owns the
relationship with the Government? If the answer is mostly the
subcontractor, that is your warning sign. If you can answer those three questions clearly,
you are usually in good shape. If you cannot, do not panic. Just
restructure the model before the Government, the SBA, or the DOJ does it for you.
Here is the big takeaway. Middleman is not a dirty word
in government contracting. Non-value middleman is the dirty word. Pass-through structures with
no substance are the dirty word. Paper prime arrangements are the dirty word.
In Part Two of this series, we are going to break down real-world red flags and case patterns that
trigger protests, ineligibility fights, audits, and the kind of misconduct allegations that put
contractors on the Department of Justice radar. And in Part Three, I will walk through the
playbook for doing this correctly. How to structure your teaming, how to price your
role as a prime, and how to explain your value in a proposal without raising compliance alarms.
Before you go, drop a comment with the number you see most often. One, two, three, or four. And tell
me your niche. IT, construction, professional services, products, whatever it is.
Build value. Own delivery. And do not be a toll booth.

Toll booths earn profit on other people’s work. Question three. If this is a set-aside, are we performing the primary and vital work and meeting the self-performance limits? Paper prime arrangements are the dirty word. Before you go, drop a comment with the number you see most often. One, two, three, or four. And tell me your niche. IT, construction, professional services, products, whatever it is. Build value. Own delivery. And do not be a toll booth.

metadata.shortDescription:
SUBSCRIBE TO WATCH THE VIDEOS FIRST https://www.youtube.com/@govclose/?sub_confirmation=1 

FREE TRAINING: https://www.govclose.com/sales-certification

GET CERTIFIED: Earn up to $400K a year as a freelance GOVERNMENT CONTRACT CONSULTANT: https://www.govclose.com/sales-certification.

Free Book Download: https://www.dodcontract.com/

Former government procurement officer Rick Howard gives an over view of subcontracting and why this niche makes big bucks for some companies.

Winning Nine-Figure Government Contracts Through Subcontracting: How We Did It
In this video, Ricky Howard explains how a client secured a nine-figure government contract as a subcontractor, detailing the benefits and strategy behind subcontracting. Ricky emphasizes the importance of being strategic, reaching out to the right companies, and establishing communication with government offices. He offers tips on effectively approaching subcontracting opportunities and discourages mass emailing tactics. Ricky also promotes the GovPost certification program, where individuals share their success stories in government contracting. Perfect for those interested in learning how to win government contracts and start their consulting business.

00:00 Introduction: Winning Big as a Subcontractor
00:12 Understanding Subcontracting vs. Prime Contracting
01:48 Common Mistakes in Subcontracting
02:51 Strategic Approach to Subcontracting
04:23 Effective Communication with Potential Partners
06:26 Success Stories and Testimonials
07:21 Conclusion and Certification Program

AskMichelleB Can I Win Contracts as a Consultant Using the Middle Man Business Model

metadata.author: GovCon Empire with Derrick Green “Theo”
metadata.shortDescription:
(FYI: Contact Info at the bottom below FAR Anchors and Description)

⚓️ FAR & Federal Law Anchors Covered
 • FAR 3.1003 – Standards of Conduct (do business above reproach)
 • FAR 9.406-2 – Causes for Debarment
 • FAR 9.407-2 – Causes for Suspension
 • FAR 44.201-1 – Consent to Subcontract
 • FAR 52.215-22 – Identification of Subcontract Effort
 • FAR 52.215-23 – Limitations on Pass-Through Charges
 • FAR 52.219-14 – Limitations on Subcontracting
 • FAR 52.244-2 – Subcontracts
 • FAR 9.601–9.604 – Contractor Team Arrangements
 • 18 U.S.C. § 1001 – False Statements
 • 18 U.S.C. § 287 – False Claims
 • 31 U.S.C. § 3729 – False Claims Act

⸻

Most people think “middleman” is a business model in government contracting.

It’s not.

In this 30-minute breakdown, I expose the difference between illegal pass-through schemes and what the FAR actually allows and why laziness, hustling, and not reading the regulations is how contractors get debarred, suspended, investigated, or worse.

I start by breaking down what gets people in trouble:
 • Paper prime fraud and pass-through charges (FAR 52.215-23)
 • Lying about who actually performs the work (FAR 52.215-22)
 • Violating limitations on subcontracting (FAR 52.219-14)
 • Charging for value you never provided
 • Misrepresenting performance during contract execution
 • Turning invoices into criminal evidence

Then, after minute 19, I break down what is ACTUALLY allowed under federal law:
 • Prime integrator / MSO models with real management value
 • Legal subcontracting with disclosure and control
 • Teaming agreements and joint ventures done the right way
 • How real contractors structure oversight, compliance, and delivery

This video also explains why ignorance is not a defense and how the FAR is built around audits, documentation, and accountability (not vibes).

⸻

📌 Watch until minute 19 to see the legal structures that actually work — and how to protect your business instead of gambling it.

If you plan to be a prime contractor, this video will save you years of pain.

metadata.title: I Won 4 Government Contracts With the Middleman Strategy…And I Regret It.
metadata.author: GovCon TechLab
metadata.shortDescription:
The GovCon middleman strategy is everywhere right now. Win the contract. Find a subcontractor. Keep the difference. And it works, I've done it four times.
But I had to come out of pocket $30,000 on a contract I had already won. And nobody told me that was coming.
In this video I break down the three things that happen between winning and getting paid that nobody puts in the tutorial: the cash flow gap, the risk you inherit as the prime contractor, and the expertise problem that keeps most middleman operators from building a real business.

I'm Stephanie Richardson Parker, 7-year active government contractor, PMP certified, WOSB/DBE/MBE certified. I manage $10-20 million in federal contract portfolios. I used this strategy. Here's what I actually learned.

WHAT'S COVERED IN THIS VIDEO:
What the middleman strategy actually is, and why the tutorials leave out the hard parts.
The $30,000 cash flow gap: what happens when the government is late paying and your sub isn't.
Why as prime contractor you own the risk; no-shows, missed deadlines, property damage, all of it.
The expertise problem: winning landscaping + HVAC + janitorial + snow removal = what business exactly?
What the middleman strategy actually gave me: past performance, confidence, relationships.
The 5 things I would do differently if I were starting over today.

Every week in our Substack newsletter we breakdown how government contracting actually works, no $3,000 courses, no guru promises. Just the real-life stories you can actually learn from.

metadata.title: Subcontracting with Prime Government Contractors is a Must
metadata.author: Neil McDonnell
metadata.shortDescription:
* Many companies think subcontracting is only for firms trying to get their first federal contract.

In reality, subcontracting is part of how work gets delivered across federal agencies.

Companies subcontract to enter new agencies, support large programs, add capabilities, or expand delivery teams.

In this live session, we’ll talk about how subcontracting actually works in the federal market. You'll learn:

• Why companies at every stage of GovCon subcontract

• How to identify prime contractors winning federal work

• How subcontracting fits into a long-term growth strategy
___________________________________

🔥 Join 28,888 others and subscribe to my GovCon newsletter | https://lnkd.in/es6qfwgk

👀 Follow me (Neil McDonnell) on LinkedIn and hit the 🔔 on my profile to see more government contracting content like 45,069 other people do.

metadata.title: How to start government contracting with 0$ |Micro Purchases
metadata.author: Federal Contracts Lab
metadata.shortDescription:
Can you win your first government contract with no cash, no credit cards, and no business loans?

In this video, I explain how beginners can start looking for government contracting opportunities through micro-purchases — smaller government buys that are often under $15,000 and may not require the same long proposal process as larger contracts.

But here’s the truth: micro-purchases are not free money, and they are not all listed on one secret website.

You’ll learn what micro-purchases are, how agencies make small purchases, and where beginners can look for clues, contacts, and opportunities.

In this video, we cover:

What micro-purchases are and why they matter for beginners
Why many micro-purchases are not posted publicly
How to use SAM.gov the right way
How to use USAspending.gov to follow small-dollar buying patterns
How to find agency small business offices through Acquisition.gov
How agency vendor portals can help you become visible
How DIBBS can help product-based businesses find smaller opportunities
Why local federal facilities can be a smart place to start
How Unison Marketplace fits into your opportunity search strategy

If you are new to government contracting and do not have money upfront, this video will help you understand how to stop chasing huge contracts you are not ready for — and start looking for smaller, more realistic entry points.

Micro-purchases are not a shortcut. They are a strategy.

Watch this video before you waste time chasing the wrong government contracts.

Subscribe for beginner-friendly government contracting tutorials, SAM.gov walkthroughs, proposal tips, and federal contracting strategy.

Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and is not legal, financial, or contracting advice. Always review official government sources and agency instructions before pursuing any opportunity.

metadata.title: Limitations on Subcontracting: Key Updates and Tips for Compliance
metadata.author: PilieroMazza PLLC
metadata.shortDescription:
The limitations on subcontracting (LOS) rules generally require that small business prime contractors self-perform 50% of supply and service contracts awarded to them, with lower self-performance percentages for different kinds of construction contracts. This requirement is applied to small business set-aside solicitations and contracts through the LOS clause at FAR 52.219-14 and seeks to prevent small businesses from becoming pass-through vehicles for large businesses. Though the reasoning for the LOS may be clear, it can be difficult to interpret how they apply to the various types of small businesses and contract vehicles. And understanding the LOS and their impact on your business can be key to maintaining compliance. Join attorneys in PilieroMazza’s Government Contracts Group as they discuss recent LOS developments, how the regulations may apply to your business, and tips for maintaining compliance.

metadata.title: Limitations on Subcontracting Rule 13 C.F.R. § 125.6 Overview and Updates to the Regulations
metadata.author: Mark Ryan
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Mark Ryan discusses the limitations on subcontracting rule and gives an overview of the rule. He talks about similarly situated entities and how the rule affects them. He talks about products, services, construction contracts and trade contracting. He talks about how a contract year works and how the requirement works with IDIQ and other multiple-award contracts.  He explains the seven exceptions that the SBA now allows.  Finally, he discusses the new changes made in 2023 and how that affects a contracting officer's requirements to leave past performance evaluations on CPARS.

metadata.title: Limitations on Subcontracting New Rules
metadata.author: PilieroMazza PLLC
metadata.shortDescription:
On July 12, 2016 we are offering a live seminar on new rules with featured speaker, John Klein, SBA’s Associate General Counsel for Procurement Law, who played a major role in drafting the final rules. That session will allow attendees to ask questions and gain valuable insight in understanding the new rules. We understand that not everyone can attend the live session and are offering this one hour webinar on July 20, 2016 on the new rule changes to be presented by Katie Flood and Megan Connor.   

The Small Business Administration recently issued its eagerly anticipated final rule to implement regulations as they relate to the limitations on subcontracting applicable to small business set-aside contracts, socioeconomic program set-aside contracts, and small business subcontracting generally. The new rules will change how to calculate compliance with the limitations on subcontracting for service and supply contracts, provide guidance on using similarly-situated subcontractors, and much more.

Topics discussed will include the rule changes to: Limitations on subcontracting, joint ventures, affiliation, annual receipts, nonmanufacturer rule, and size protests.

PilieroMazza materials appearing on our website (www.pilieromazza.com) and other webpages have been prepared by PilieroMazza to generally inform visitors about our law firm and legal developments that may be of interest to them. Viewers should not rely on these materials as legal advice about specific legal issues and these materials are not guaranteed to be complete, correct, or up-to-date. Such advice can be rendered only contemporaneously and by counsel familiar with the complete facts and circumstances involved. You should not act upon the information on this website or webpage without consulting with legal counsel. Posting and viewing of these materials is not intended to constitute the rendering of legal advice or to create any attorney-client relationship with the viewer.

metadata.title: GovCon 101   Federal Acquisition Regulation FAR
metadata.author: Public Contracting Institute (PCI)
metadata.shortDescription:
The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) is an exceedingly-complex document; but it is also the primary regulation which governs most federal agency procurements. The FAR’s purpose is to ensure the government’s procurement procedures are consistent, and conducted in an impartial manner, while fairly balancing risks between the government and the contractor. Knowing what’s in the FAR, and how it’s organized, is essential for all contracting professionals.

Learning Objectives:

To understand the overall organization and content of the FAR
To understand the relationship between the FAR’s substantive parts, and its corresponding clauses and provisions.
To understand the mandatory and optional (i.e., negotiable) aspects of the FAR.
Instructor: David Drabkin, Drabkin & Associates

And now if you are simply I don't mean simply, but if you're providing only commercial products and services, don't have to worry about these things. Contract finance maybe maybe your contract is one that would be eligible for progress payments because you're building an airplane and final delivery is not going to place take place till eight years and you need money to keep going all the way along, you would do that through progress payments. Part 33 part 33 covers protests and disputes which we've talked about a little bit. It's all laid out in far part 33. And far part 33 is also where we have something called ADR, alternative dispute resolution. Now it's one lousy paragraph, but boy is it a big part of our government contracting community now in terms of resolving disputes between suppliers and customers without burning the bridges down between them. Alternative dispute resolution. Major systems acquisitions are covered, construction and architectural engineering contracts are covered. So they need to do an A&E contract which is covered in its own part of the far and has its own rules. segments.text: A government customer asks your team to
start extra work. Before anyone says
yes, your first question should be about
authority, not enthusiasm. FAR Part 1
explains the acquisition regulatory
system and contracting authority.
Contracting officers bind the government
only within their delegated authority. A
contracting officer's representative
supports monitoring and administration
within a written designation. That role
does not carry authority to change
contractual price, quantity, delivery,
or other terms. Before applying this to
a real acquisition, check the current
FAR, the agency's applicable deviation,
and the solicitation or contract. The
codified text and overhaul model may use
different section numbers. A job title,
a relationship, or an urgent request
does not establish authority to
authorize a contract change.
Ratification is a separate process with
conditions. It is not a dependable
business plan for work started without
proper authorization. Consider a
hypothetical engineering supplier asked
by a technical contact to add testing
outside its existing scope. Its project
lead records the request, compares it
with the current requirement, and sends
the issue through the company's
contracts lead to the contracting
officer. The team identifies possible
cost and schedule effects before
promising a change. This example
illustrates a control. It does not
decide the rights or duties under a
particular contract. Build a contact and
authority sheet for one active
engagement. Identify the contracting
officer, the designated technical
representative, your authorized company
signer, and your internal escalation
owner. Keep the current award,
modifications, and delegations available
to the people who need them. Have staff
explain where they would send a request
that might change scope. A clear
authority path helps your team respond
promptly without making commitments
based on assumptions. Dove Assessment
provides a structured business readiness
baseline based on your answers. It does
not certify compliance or guarantee an
award. Explore the review levels at
govsuccess.com.
Subscribe to govsuccess for the next FAR
part explained in practical language.

metadata.title: GovCon 101 - A Guide to Navigating FAR Part 52
metadata.author: Public Contracting Institute (PCI)
metadata.shortDescription:
The FAR is a big book, filled with hundreds of policies and prescriptions designed to protect the taxpayer and enforce federal law. These policies and prescriptions are typically implemented in a government contract through the FAR Part 52 contract clauses, which provide a listing of more than 600 different contract clauses – many of which you will likely find in your government contracts. This session of GovCon 101 provides an overview of FAR Part 52 and the government’s standard contract clauses. This session will also touch on how you can use FAR part 52 to identify which contract clauses will apply to your project (including sometimes alternates or deviations), and also when these contract clauses need to be flowed down to subcontractors. Join our expert instructor, David Gallacher (Kutak Rock LLP) as he walks you through the basics relating to FAR Part 52 contract clauses.

videos.full_text: Thank you for joining Jennifer Shatz and Associates in our 2019 Webinar Wednesday series. We're coming to you live from downtown Washington, D.C. Our webinars are every Wednesday and you can find the upcoming schedule on our website. Past webinars and all recordings are also on our website and on our YouTube channel along with 160 other recordings on federal contracting topics. All are complimentary. If you have questions for our speaker today, you can email her directly. The contact information you'll see on the last slide. All right, this is just a little bit about us. We are Washington D.C. based firm and provide services to federal contractors. This ranges from market analysis support to proposal writing and also post award compliance. More information is on our website, please visit us there. We do offer advertising in our newsletter. So, you can email this email if you'd like more information on that. All right, our speaker today is Devine Hewitt. She's going to be covering FAR compliance, what every sub needs to know. Thank you for joining us today and I'm going to go ahead and hand it over to you. Thank you. Uh good morning and and thank you for calling in to to hear about this topic. In order to uh determine what every sub needs to know about FAR compliance, the contractor or the subcontractor needs to know what the FAR is um and whether a particular provision of the FAR applies to it to the subcontractor um and then how to comply with that FAR provision and the risks of doing so. And that's the way I'm going to proceed here. Next slide. What is the FAR? The FAR stands for Federal Acquisition Regulation and it is the um regulation that applies generally speaking to procurements by uh executive agencies of the United States government. Um there the actual app applicability of the FAR provisions um uh go to acquisitions, executive agencies, and appropriated funds. Those are the three talismans of what, um, what triggers FAR application. Now, the FAR applies to, uh, agencies and representatives of agencies. It doesn't directly apply to contractors. However, the FAR does require contracting officers and contracting personnel to include various clauses and provisions in government contracts and and particularly prime contracts because the government doesn't have a direct relationship which, um, the specific term is called privity, with subcontractors, but the contracting personnel do have a obligation to include certain FAR clauses and provisions in prime contracts. And the difference between the term claw, uh, provisions and clauses, um, is important. Provisions, um, uh, solicitation provisions are, uh, provisions that are included in solicitations that, uh, apply to the procurement itself. And then generally delete or fall out of the, uh, solicitation once a contract has been awarded. And FAR clauses, the term clauses, applies to clauses that remain in the prime contract. So, clauses affect, uh, performance. Provisions, solicitation provisions, uh, affect the procurement, but they both, both types of, uh, provisions or both types of language comes from the FAR. Now, many of these FAR clauses, and by that I mean, uh, provisions that are included that remain in the contract and affect contract performance, also require the prime to quote-unquote flow down the FAR clause to its subcontractors. And that's known in the industry as mandatory flow down clauses. Other FAR clauses um uh are discretionary by the government or contracting personnel. Uh they are required to put in these quote-unquote mandatory clauses in the prime contract, but they also include other clauses that are not absolutely required by the FAR, but are but that the FAR instructs them to do so in various context or types of procurements or a certain value of procurements. So, a prime contract will include these mandatory FAR clauses, as well as these other discretionary clauses that apply in different contexts. And to the extent there are these discretionary clauses in the prime contract uh or a clause in the prime contract or does not mandate that the prime flow that down to the sub, the choice of whether the prime will flow down to its subcontractor is also discretionary to the prime or you know, subject uh to inclusion depending on the negotiations between the prime and the sub. So, the most important thing here is to recognize that a subcontract is really a mixture of a government contract and a commercial contract. Um in one uh sense, it is just simply a contract between two businesses um in a commercial transaction where standard commercial terms apply and um you know, a choice of law provision is included making whatever state law applicable. But on the other hand, a federal subcontract also will have a number of references or clauses that stem from this regulation that applies to procurement the federal government generally, then applies to a prime contractor and then flows down to the sub. So, becoming a subcontractor does not mean that you are only going to be uh faced with commercial provisions with which you might um or have to comply, there are also this other rubric that would apply to the transaction and which may or may not be apparent uh when you enter into the subcontract. Next slide. So, the first um thing also other than to figure out what the FAR is, is to determine whether or not you're a subcontractor because as I mentioned um in the prime contract, there will be clauses included by the government which by their own language state that the prime contractor has to flow it down to the subcontractor. And so, it will say pretty much in the last paragraph of that FAR clause, it will say to the prime contractor, "Include the substance uh or substantially similar substance of this clause in your subcontract." But for a prime or a potential sub sub, how do you know whether or not you actually fit that definition of a subcontractor and whether or not that needs to be flowed down in your particular transaction with the prime. And both the prime and the sub uh need to know this. Now, I will tell you that in the industry, the prime contractor typically flows everything down just to be safe, but from a subcontractor point of view, what subcontractors need to know is that not all of clauses clauses that a prime might flow down are actually required to be flowed down or are necessary in the context of the contract to be flowed down. So, the one of the most important thing for a sub to realize is that yes, there are certain clauses the prime must include in your subcontract and the requirement does not extend to other prime contracts. But, in order to be within the ambit of that required flow down, you have to determine whether you indeed are a {quote} {unquote} subcontractor. And this is difficult under the FAR. Um, there was a procurement reform uh panel that was authorized by Congress several several years ago and some parts of it are still ongoing. It's known as the section 809 panel. And the 809 panel issued a report and said that the FAR and the DFARS, which is the Department of Defense FAR Supplement, have 27 {quote} {unquote} separate, sometimes overlapping definitions of subcontractor. And so, sometimes companies are indeed subcontractors without realizing it. Now, if you have a contract with a a a prime contractor and it includes FAR clauses, I there's a presumption that you indeed are a subcontractor as that term is used in a particular FAR clause. But, that may not be true because of these various definitions. And the definitions may shift depending on the nature or the context of the clause. And for example, subcontractors or vendors or other companies that have contracts with a prime contractor may be considered subcontractors for example affirmative action equal employment opportunity veterans recruitment a lot of the socioeconomic clauses flow down to a variety of organizations that may interact with a prime contractor but that are not {quote} specifically subcontractors as most people would define that term. The common approach and what most companies are used to is that any contractor that is providing either goods or services identified in the prime contract statement of work is a subcontractor. And so that type of relationship is pretty easy to recognize. If if your company is doing some of the work and that's being um provided to the government you are a subcontractor and most likely the document you have um with the prime will include some far clauses. Now a question often arises um with regard to a subcontractor um it it knows that the far clauses that apply to it apply to it as an entity and to its employees but are consultants 1099s are they subcontractors to it? Are they what's known second tier subcontractors? Or are they considered vendors and um not otherwise subject to these flow downs? Conventional wisdom says again that consultants who are assisting your company or a contracting company in performing part of the statement of work are also subcontractors and may be viewed as subcontractors to you with respect to a a of these far clauses but it may be that from the Department of Labor context, for example, that consultants are treated differently. So, the the biggest takeaway here is that it's not always clear um on the margins whether or not certain FAR clauses may apply to a particular company. Again, contractors that provide part of the scope of work, that's fairly clear. And I think it's also clear that if contractors that provide goods and services that benefit the company um as a whole or even enable the company to perform the work uh are probably not subcontractors. Another way to look at this is to look at what is a direct expense on the contract and what is an indirect expense. So, for example, uh your lease costs for your offices or your technology costs, um your you know, security costs, whatever uh an office as a general procures for its operations is likely not going to be a subcontractor. But yet, there are exceptions, and in particular, Department of Labor Affirmative Action Equal Employment Opportunity, the Department of Labor defines subcontractor differently. So, that's an area um for which contractors and subcontractors need to be particularly sensitive to. Next slide. Now, as I said, there are two types of FAR clauses that ultimately are in a prime contract. From the government's perspective, there are certain ones they have to include, and then there are other ones that they should include given the context of the procurement. The same uh standard applies to prime contractors. There are clauses in the prime contract that they must flow down to the subcontractors, and then there are clauses that they feel they must flow down, not because the term of that FAR clause requires it, but because in order to comply with that FAR clause in the prime contract, they have to get commitments or require their subcontractors to perform or or meet the same standard. As I mentioned, the mandatory clauses are easy to spot. Actually, they have text in the clause instructing the prime contractor to flow down the substance of the clause to subcontractors. Now, the fact that it is a mandatory flow down clause does not actually mean that it is applicable to the subcontract work. In the best of all worlds, a prime would flow down those clauses it is required to flow down, but only in the context in which that flow down requirement appears. So, for example, FAR clauses in the prime contract may only apply to contracts above or below certain dollar thresholds, may only apply to certain types of contracts like fixed price, cost reimbursement, may apply to only certain types of work or certain certain nature of the work. Is it a commercial item? So, the fact that a prime says to a sub, "Well, this is a mandatory flow down." doesn't mean that in fact it is a mandatory flow down that is applicable to what you are doing. So, again, subs have to be aware of the distinction between mandatory and discretionary, and then when it's mandatory between whether or not that mandatory clause is in fact mandatory with respect to the work that subcontractor or entity is doing for the prime contractor. What subs also don't realize is that discretionary clauses can be negotiated. Now, of course, that depends on the subcontractor's leverage with the prime, but if a prime flows down the clause that it believes the subcontractor needs to comply with in order for it to comply with its obligations, then a prime is going to be reluctant to alter the text of that clause. But in other cases, the text really needs to be altered in order for the prime to um to actually comply with the clause in its prime contract. So, for example, uh Buy America Act, that is a standard FAR clause if you're providing um certain kinds of and I'll use the term widgets to the government, and you can only use materials uh in that widget or that product you're giving to the government that actually have been manufactured in the United States. Now, there are a bunch of exceptions under something called the Trade Agreements Act, but in order to comply with that, you need to make your make sure your subcontractor is only buying America as well. But it may be that the Buy America provision only applies to certain types of materials or minerals from certain countries. And it may be that in the role you're playing, that doesn't apply. Or it may apply to only part of it. So, again, it may be appropriate to negotiate it. Um or it may be appropriate to say this really doesn't apply. More importantly, a lot of these clauses contain blanks or time frames that need to be altered. Um what you know, the common one is the substitution paragraph because the FAR clauses are written with terms that reflect the contracting officer and the contractor in that context, the prime contractor. But if it gets flowed down, it should reflect the relationship between the prime contractor and the subcontractor. But there are blanks for certain kinds of items or certain kinds of amounts. Lo- Most likely, the blanks have to do with timing. If you have to submit a claim within 30 days, do you want your subcontractor to give it to you on the 30th day? That may not give you enough time to turn it around. So you may want to ask the subcontractor to do it a little earlier, and the subcontractor needs to understand that as well. So the point here is that the FAR clauses are somewhat dynamic, even if they're mandatory, and they do bear a second look, which many subcontractors don't do. It is a resource allocation issue. They're complicated, and I'll talk later about how primes just flow everything down and put the burden on the subcontractor, but I do think it's something um worth doing. Next slide. Most primes flow everything down. Um and you typically get an appendix with all the FAR clauses, and then there's a substitution paragraph. Uh sometimes, actually, FAR clauses will flow down that are not included in the prime contractor under something called the Christian doctrine. So there may be even obligations that you're not aware of uh and you're held to them. And all I can say in that regard is again, it's most likely the socioeconomic obligations that are otherwise imposed by statute, and maybe some of the other um you know, benefit society type of provisions, clean air, clean water, uh drug-free workplace, etc. Next slide. So here are the risks. When you flow down all these clauses to the sub, the sub now has the burden to decide what to do about these. As I've mentioned, some of those are mandatory, and there's really not much the far the subcontractor can do, except what it can do is say, "All right, I'll accept all the mandatory flow downs if applicable." So, that's a negotiation term they can include in the subcontract. They also can look at those far mandatory provisions and decide if there any blanks or substitution issues that need to be enclosed in order to make sense. And then there are all the other clauses that are desirable or otherwise just flowed down because the government itself hasn't um had the discipline to go through and actually identify those clauses that are applicable and necessary for the particular procurement. The prime's going to push that down. You can look at those clauses, and to the extent you think they're going to make a real impact, you could try to negotiate. Again, you could um you know, fill in the blanks, or you could again say as applicable. But, there is one particular risk that I both primes and subs I don't think have a full appreciation. Uh and that is order of precedence precedence. You're going to have all these this appendix with all these far clauses. And then you're going to have the subcontract. And in the subcontract, you will probably negotiate on some issues or topics that are also reflected in the far flow down clauses. Now, unless you are spending a good amount of time, you know, using a a fine-tooth comb to go through the entire subcontract, it is likely that there there will be some conflict in the text of a far clause versus the text of the actual subcontract. And usually in the subcontract, there'll be an order of precedence. It says if there is a conflict, either the FAR provision will trump what's in the subcontract or the subcontract provision will trump what's in the um FAR clause. The problem is that that may result in something that the parties did not intend. For example, disputes clause. The FAR disputes clause um sets out a a manner uh pursuant to which a prime contractor can submit a claim to the government in accordance with various procedures. Now, the the prime contractor does not have to flow that down, but it may just cuz it's part of you know, its entire flow-down package, and it could rely on that text for the purposes of the sub submitting a claim that it would transfer and otherwise turn around and submit to the government. But that text doesn't really address disputes between the sub and the prime. So the sub and the prime may include a provision, a disputes provision in the subcontract, which um addresses sub-prime disputes or sub-prime disputes and prime-government disputes and prime sponsorship of subcontractor claims. If that's the case, then which governs? The FAR disputes clause that's incorporated by reference or the process for submitting claims to the government included in the prime contract? And also, the disputes clause, the FAR disputes clause, may not say that you have to continue to perform, whereas the prime contractor will absolutely want the subcontractor to continue to perform while a dispute is pending. So those are issues that can arise in inconsistency. To make it worse, the FAR there is a FAR clause that in of itself has an order of precedence of clauses flowed down. So, now you have two levels of order of precedence. The same issue is going to apply, for example, for data rights, IP provisions. The standard FAR IP provisions require the contractor to give the government certain licenses. Now, that'll be flowed down most likely to a sub if they're providing intellectual property. But, and the but from the prime's perspective, they're going to want to take all the ownership of IP, and their standard commercial contract is going to include something like a work-for-hire provision where they take all IP rights in the IP that's produced by a subcontractor. However, the FAR clause only says that the sub has to give the government a license. Now, the prime contractor may use the substitution paragraph to um to, you know, substitute its position for the contracting officer's position, but as a matter of fact, the only end user is the government, and the prime may not have a need to have that. So, an awareness of that allows a subcontractor to either modify the prime contractor to take into account the FAR clause or take into account a certain part of it, or to say that this IP clause in the contract takes precedence over the FAR clause. Again, many subs are not aware of these inconsistency and the impact or the consequences of an order of precedence clause if there is a conflict. Next slide. So, ultimately, these are the best practices that I recommend for a sub. You know, there are blanket statements often not even with an appendix, where a prime will say a sub is has to comply with all the requirements that the prime has to comply with. That's outrageous. Just reject that. You know, if you have to accept it, say all applicable requirements. Typically, I say turn over the prime contract. How do you expect me to comply with the prime contract if I don't have it? And many many primes are not willing to do that. So, say say at a minimum you'll comply with whatever is in your contract. And then, if you get all those FAR clauses, and they don't allow you to actually negotiate them, what you can do again is say, "Okay, I'll accept the flow down, but only as applicable." Because that will give you an ability say, "Hey, this FAR clause is not applicable to me." You can modify that substitution paragraph to say, "Well, certain ones the substitution for contracting officer for government will apply, but not in these cases, i.e., intellectual property." Or you may allow the government to audit if the government does have the right to audit your your, you know, expenses related to a contract, but you may not want the prime to audit. Or with respect to government property. If you are taking care of government property, your issues are really with the government, not with the prime. You can strike those clauses that are clearly inapplicable. You know, the prime may say, "Well, if it's not applicable, it won't matter." You know, at the end of the day, the right thing is to strike it, but you may have to pick other battles. And remember you can negotiate clauses of discretionary FAR clauses, and you may need to do so because of blanks included in there or substitutions that don't work. But really the most important thing out of all these best practices is to identify potentially inconsistent far versus subcontract provisions that are very important whether it's payment disputes changes intellectual property termination all those commercial standard terms could actually conflict with far terms and that absolutely needs to be resolved in any subcontract negotiation. That's it. Thank you. Thank you for tuning in today. If you have any questions you can reach out to us via the email or phone number shown on the screen and this webcast is now over. Thank you.

metadata.title: FAR Subpart 3.4 - Contingent Fees
metadata.author: Frank Reilly
metadata.shortDescription:
Referenced case law:

Section 2306(b) of title 10, United States Code, places certain limitations on obtaining contracts under “contingent fee” arrangements. However, the purpose of this limitation, as implemented by Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) subpart 3.4, is to prevent the attempted or actual exercise of improper influence by third parties over the federal procurement system. Puma Industrial Consulting v. Daal Assocs., Inc., 808 F.2d 89 (2d Cir. 1987); Quinn v. Gulf & Western Corp., 644 F.2d 89 (2d Cir. 1981); E&R, Inc.--Claim for Costs, B‑255868.2, May 30, 1996, 96-1 CPD para. 264 at 3-4; Howard Johnson Lodge--Recon., B‑244302.2, Mar. 24, 1992, 92-1 CPD para. 305. We have held that the prohibition applies only to situations where an agent agrees “to solicit or obtain” a contract from a procuring agency. Bertsch Constr., B‑253526, Aug. 25, 1993, 93-2 CPD para. 122. The fact that an agent’s fee is contingent upon the contractor’s successful performance of the contract, or even upon receiving the contract award, is not sufficient, by itself, to bring a fee agreement under the contingent fee prohibition; rather, the regulation contemplates a specific demonstration that an agent is retained for the express purpose of contacting government officials, where such contact poses a threat of the exertion of improper influence to obtain government contracts. Convention Mktg. Servs., B‑245660.3, B‑246175, Feb. 4, 1992, 92-1 CPD para. 144. Here, Kola Nut acknowledges that the consultant’s fee agreement is calculated as a portion of the profit resulting from the awardees’ performance of the contract--not in exchange for the awardees’ receipt of contract awards. Kola Nut Protest Submission (Mar. 28, 2005) at 3. Further, the record is devoid of any evidence that the challenged awards reflect any improper influence on government officials. To the contrary, as shown above, the agency selected proposals that offered significantly lower prices and were evaluated equal to, or higher than, Kola Nut’s proposal with regard to the non-price evaluation factors. On this record, Kola Nut’s assertion that the contracts incorporate a prohibited contingent fee agreement is without merit. (Kola Nut Travel, Inc., B-296090.4, August 25, 2005)

videos.full_text: [Music] contractors arrangements to pay contingent fees for soliciting or obtaining government contracts have long been considered contrary to public policy because such arrangements may lead to attempted or actual exercise of improper influence congress affirmed this public policy but did permit certain exceptions in general federal law requires in every negotiated contract a warranty by the contractor against contingent fees but federal law does permit as an exception to this warranty contingent fee arrangements between contractors and bona fide employees or bonafide agencies and these statutes provide that for breach or violation of the warranty by the contractor the government may annul the contract without liability or deduct the contract price or consideration or otherwise recover the full amount of the contingent fee government personnel who suspect or have evidence of attempted or actual exercise of improper influence misrepresentation of a contingent fee arrangement or other violation of the covenant against contingent fees shall report the matter promptly to the contracting officer or appropriate hire authority in accordance with agency procedures where there is specific evidence or other reasonable basis to suspect one or more violations the chief contracting officer shall review the facts and if appropriate take or direct one or more of the following or other actions if the situation is before award reject the bidder proposal if the situation is after award enforce the government's right to annul the contract or to recover the fee and or initiate suspension or debarment and or refer suspected fraudulent or criminal matters to the department of justice as prescribed in agency regulations in the matter of cola nut travel incorporated the protester alleged that there was a prohibited contingency fee arrangement the gao noted that it is held that the prohibition applies only to situations where an agent agrees to solicit or obtain a contract from a procuring agency the fact that an agent's fee is contingent upon the contractor's successful performance of the contract or even upon receiving the contract award is not sufficient by itself to bring a fee agreement under the contingent fee prohibition rather the regulation contemplates a specific demonstration that an agent is retained for the express purpose of contacting government officials where such contact poses a threat of the exertion of improper influence to obtain government contracts in this case it was determined that the consultant's fee agreement was calculated as a portion of the profit resulting from the awardee's performance of the contract not in exchange for the awardee's receipt of contract awards in addition the gao noted that the record was devoid of any evidence that the challenged awards reflect any improper influence on government officials to the contrary the gao determined that the agency selected proposals that offered significantly lower prices and were evaluated equal to or higher than the protesters proposal with regard to the non-price evaluation factors based on the records submitted the gao determined that the protesters assertion that the contracts incorporated a prohibited contingency fee arrangement were without merit [Music]

metadata.title: The New Rules of Federal Buying: How the FAR Overhaul Is Changing Everything
metadata.author: Fed Gov Today
metadata.shortDescription:
Matthew Rose, Head of Government Affairs at Snowflake, joins Fed Gov Today to discuss how the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) overhaul is transforming the way government buys technology and services. He explains that recent changes mark a major cultural shift in communication between agencies and industry, encouraging open dialogue and collaboration during market research. These updates, he says, are helping both sides keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI and data technologies.
Rose highlights three key trends emerging from the overhaul: stronger communication, broader engagement with diverse vendors, and reduced complexity in acquisition. He notes that agencies are increasingly adopting outcome-based contracting—focusing on results rather than level of effort—which mirrors best practices from the commercial world. This approach allows the government to better leverage its immense buying power and streamline procurement through initiatives like One Gov.
He stresses that leadership and education are critical to sustaining these changes. Agency leaders must help their teams revisit old assumptions and understand how new technologies, including AI, can improve both mission outcomes and day-to-day work. Rose concludes that the ultimate goal is simpler, faster acquisitions that deliver greater value for agencies, industry partners, and taxpayers alike.

segments.text: Your company paid the invoice.
Does that mean the Government should reimburse the charge?
A real business expense still needs the right contractual
basis and supporting evidence.
This is GovSuccess.
Today we are making the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) practical
through FAR Part 31: Contract Cost Principles and Procedures.
We will separate applicability, allowability, reasonableness,
and allocability, then use a hypothetical shared-cost example
to turn those ideas into a review your team can actually perform.
Start with applicability.
explains how the commercial-organization cost principles are used in cost analysis,
reimbursement, indirect rates, and other specified cost determinations.
A commercial organization is not the same concept as a commercial
product or commercial service.
Identify the transaction and the contract terms before choosing
the applicable cost framework.
A fixed-price award does not turn every expense into a
separately reimbursable item.
Pricing a modification and requesting reimbursement are different transactions,
even when both involve cost information.
identifies five allowability conditions: reasonableness, allocability, applicable
accounting standards, contract terms, and limitations in the cost principles.
Passing one condition does not settle the rest.
Reasonableness asks whether the nature and amount make sense for
a prudent competitive business.
Under FAR 31.201-3,
spending the money does not create a presumption that the amount is reasonable.
Allocability asks which work benefits.
connects the assignment of a cost with relative benefit or another
equitable relationship, including costs that benefit more than one activity.
The accounting condition includes applicable Cost Accounting
Standards, or otherwise the appropriate generally accepted
accounting principles and practices.
Keep that question separate from deciding whether a specific cost is allowable.
Then check the contract and the cost principle for the particular expense.
A reasonable, properly allocated amount can still encounter a
contractual restriction or a specific allowability limitation.
This lesson uses the codified FAR text displayed on Acquisition.gov.
Check the applicable agency deviation and the actual contract before using any
section reference in a live decision.
Overhaul model text and an agency's implemented deviation
are not interchangeable.
Save the version and effective date you reviewed so the next person can
trace the basis for your decision.
Here is a hypothetical example.
A company pays $2,000 to maintain shared test equipment used by four projects.
Its estimator wants to charge the full invoice to one Government job.
Equal division is not automatically correct either.
Suppose supported usage records show that the Government job received
one quarter of the relevant benefit.
That suggests a $500 allocation to investigate, not automatic approval.
The team still checks its consistent accounting treatment, the maintenance
cost principle, contract restrictions, and evidence that the price is reasonable.
Keep the invoice, usage records, calculation, and review together.
Do not confuse a necessary business expense with an
allowable Government charge.
Your internal budget approval is useful management evidence; it does not replace
the cost principles or contract terms.
addresses identification and exclusion of expressly unallowable or mutually
agreed unallowable costs, including relevant directly associated costs.
An indirect-cost pool does not make an unallowable expense disappear.
Maintain a visible trail between the ledger and the claimed amount.
If a reviewer cannot see the purpose, allocation, and applicable basis, the file
is not ready for a confident decision.
Build a cost-support sheet with five fields: transaction and purpose;
applicable contract and cost principle; accounting treatment and
allocation basis; supporting records; and reviewer with review date.
Ask finance to explain the numbers, operations to explain the benefit, and
contracts to check the governing terms.
Resolve a disagreement before the amount moves into a proposal, billing, or claim.
These are GovSuccess preparation steps, not a Government
allowability determination.
For a difficult interpretation or material exposure, obtain qualified
accounting or legal advice and use the appropriate contractual channel.
Your takeaways are simple: identify the applicable framework, apply every
allowability condition, and retain evidence that connects the expense
to the amount you propose or claim.
GovAssessment provides a structured business-readiness
baseline based on your answers.
It does not approve costs, certify compliance, or guarantee an award.
Explore the review levels at govsuccess dot com.
Use this lesson to review one actual cost transaction with the people who own
the contract and the accounting records.
This is general education, not legal or tax advice.
Subscribe to GovSuccess for more practical FAR lessons.

segments.text: An award can make your backlog look strong while your bank
balance tells a different story.
When does the contract actually let
you request payment?
This is GovSuccess, and today we are making the Federal Acquisition
Regulation (FAR) practical through FAR Part 32: Contract
Financing.
We will distinguish financing from invoice payments and build a cash-flow
check around documented triggers rather than an optimistic award announcement.
FAR Part 32 addresses financing and payment matters across
different contract arrangements.
defines contract financing as an authorized Government disbursement before
acceptance of supplies or services.
It includes several financing methods, not one universal payment program.
A purchase-order total, a funded amount, a financing
authorization, and cash collected are different facts.
Read the clauses and payment instructions before treating any of
them as money available for payroll.
Cost-based progress payments and performance-based payments
use different triggers.
ties performance-based financing to events or measurable criteria
identified in the contract; an internal milestone does not
create that entitlement by itself.
Invoice-payment timing is a separate question.
generally connects the due date to a proper invoice and acceptance,
subject to its exceptions and other
applicable rules.
Do not turn that general framework into a promise that every
invoice is paid a fixed number of
days after you email it.
Identify who receives the invoice, what makes it proper, and what
evidence establishes acceptance.
This lesson uses the codified FAR text displayed on Acquisition.gov.
Check the applicable agency deviation and your solicitation or
contract before applying a section.
An overhaul model is not automatically the text your agency has implemented.
Keep the source, effective date, and solicitation amendment
with your decision record.
Imagine a supplier building specialized test units.
It must buy components and pay technicians before delivery.
Its draft forecast shows a payment when its own
design review finishes, but the contract's financing event requires a
different, documented accomplishment.
The team corrects the forecast, identifies the submission and approval steps, and
models the remaining cash gap.
A second scenario assumes a reasonable administrative delay.
These are business forecasts, not interpretations that
create a new payment right.
An invoice is a request, not proof that acceptance occurred.
Likewise, authorization for one financing method does not
authorize every other method.
Track what
has been submitted, approved, withheld, liquidated, and collected
so financing is not counted twice as revenue or available cash.
If the terms are unclear,
raise the specific issue with the contracting officer through the
proper channel; do not silently replace the clause with your
preferred commercial payment terms.
Build a payment-trigger worksheet.
For each expected receipt, record the clause and contract line item,
the trigger, supporting evidence, submission route, acceptance or
approval owner, forecast date, and actual receipt.
Place the related supplier and payroll outflows beside it.
Ask contracts, finance, and delivery to reconcile
the dates before committing resources.
The takeaway is operational: a forecast should explain how
performance becomes an authorized request and then collected cash.
Use the exercise with one real opportunity and assign an owner
to every unresolved question.

answers; it does not certify compliance
or guarantee an award.

Keep the source, effective date, and solicitation amendment with your decision record. Imagine a supplier building specialized test units. It must buy components and pay technicians before delivery. Its draft forecast shows a payment when its own design review finishes, but the contract's financing event requires a different, documented accomplishment. The team corrects the forecast, identifies the submission and approval steps, and models the remaining cash gap. A second scenario assumes a reasonable administrative delay. These are business forecasts, not interpretations that create a new payment right. An invoice is a request, not proof that acceptance occurred. Likewise, authorization for one financing method does not authorize every other method. Track what has been submitted, approved, withheld, liquidated, and collected so financing is not counted twice as revenue or available cash. If the terms are unclear, raise the specific issue with the contracting officer through the proper channel; do not silently replace the clause with your preferred commercial payment terms. Build a payment-trigger worksheet. For each expected receipt, record the clause and contract line item, the trigger, supporting evidence, submission route, acceptance or approval owner, forecast date, and actual receipt. Place the related supplier and payroll outflows beside it. Ask contracts, finance, and delivery to reconcile the dates before committing resources. The takeaway is operational: a forecast should explain how performance becomes an authorized request and then collected cash. Use the exercise with one real opportunity and assign an owner to every unresolved question. GovAssessment provides a structured business-readiness baseline based on your answers; it does not certify compliance or guarantee an award. Explore the review levels at govsuccess dot com. This is general education, not legal or tax advice. Subscribe to GovSuccess for more practical FAR lessons.

The federal government is under pressure to move faster.

Less delay.
Less outdated process.
More speed.
More practical buying.
More results.

In this episode of GovCon Empire, Derrick Green breaks down what the FAR (Federal Acquisition Regulation) is, why agencies are being pushed to buy faster, and what businesses need to do right now to stay competitive.

We cover:

• What the FAR is in plain English
• Why procurement delays cost taxpayers money
• FAR Part 12 commercial buying explained
• FAR Part 10 market research explained
• FAR Part 13 simplified acquisitions explained
• FAR Part 6 competition requirements explained
• FAR Part 42 post-award execution explained
• Why prepared companies will win more work
• How to respond to RFPs, RFQs, RFIs, and ITBs
• Quick update on GSA modernization

Government contracting is not getting casual.

It is getting smarter.

The companies that win next will not be the loudest.

They will be the most ready.

metadata.title: Understanding FAR Compliance
metadata.author: NSBGCA
metadata.shortDescription:
This presentation provides a practical introduction to Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) compliance for businesses supporting federal contracts and subcontracts. It explains the FAR’s purpose and applicability, including the way contract clauses may flow down to subcontractors, and outlines key compliance areas: ethics, cybersecurity and safeguarding of sensitive information, financial accounting and cost principles, contract pricing, labor requirements, and socioeconomic programs.

Attendees will gain an awareness of common FAR-driven responsibilities and the internal practices that can help support compliance, such as reviewing contract-specific clauses, maintaining effective accounting and internal-control processes, training personnel, and seeking clarification from the contracting officer or prime contractor when needed. The session also addresses potential financial, contractual, and reputational consequences of noncompliance, helping small businesses better recognize and manage compliance risk as they pursue and perform federal work.
