Real Questions. Real Scenarios. Real Presales.

Learn practical Cloud Presales, Infrastructure Presales, Solution Architecture, RFP/RFI/RFQ, Bid Management, HLD/LLD, BoQ, Sizing, Cloud Migration, Data Center, Managed Services and Cybersecurity.

metadata.title: How to Build a Tender Compliance Matrix in 6 Steps
metadata.author: Bid and Comply
metadata.shortDescription:
Most tenders are not lost on price. They are lost on compliance. In this video you will learn how to build a tender compliance matrix in 6 practical steps, so every requirement is answered, backed by evidence and easy for the evaluator to find.

Who this is for: bid managers, proposal writers and contractors responding to tenders, RFPs and RFQs for government, UN, oil and gas, security and engineering contracts.

Chapters:
0:00 Why tenders are lost
0:22 What a compliance matrix is
0:45 Step 1: Read the whole tender pack
1:10 Step 2: One requirement per row
1:32 Step 3: Mandatory or scored
1:53 Step 4: Map each requirement to your answer
2:31 Step 5: Assign owners and track status
2:50 Step 6: Independent check before submission
3:10 3 common mistakes
3:46 Final tips
4:03 The compliance matrix template

Get the Tender Compliance Matrix template (editable Excel, with guidance on every column): https://bidandcomply.com
Ready to use templates with guidance on every section: https://bidandcomply.com
Bid writing and tender support: https://bidandcomply.com/bidwriting.html

Follow Bid and Comply:
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/bidandcomply
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/bidandcomply
Pinterest: https://www.pinterest.com/bidandcomply

Subscribe for practical tender, bid and compliance tips every week.

#tender #bidwriting #compliance

segments.text: Most tenders are not lost on price.
They are lost on compliance.
A missing form, a requirement answered in the wrong place, or a mandatory
document nobody noticed.
In the next five minutes, you will learn how to build a tender compliance
matrix, the one document that stops this from happening.
A compliance matrix is a simple table.
It lists every requirement in the tender, and for each one it shows where
you answered it, what evidence you provided, and who is responsible.
Evaluators score what they can find.
A compliance matrix makes sure they find everything, and it shows you the
gaps before the client does.
Step one.
Read the whole tender pack, not just the scope of work.
Requirements hide everywhere: in the instructions to bidders, the technical
specification, the health, safety and environment appendix, the contract
terms, and every clarification the client issues.
Collect all of these documents in one folder before you start.
Step two.
Pull out every requirement, one per row.
Look for the words must, shall, will, and required.
Each one is a commitment the evaluator will check.
Give every requirement a reference number, and copy the client's exact
words, so nobody can argue later about what was asked.
Step three.
Mark each requirement as mandatory or scored.
Mandatory items are pass or fail.
Miss one, and your bid can be rejected before anyone reads your technical proposal.
Scored items earn points, so they tell you where to spend your best writing time.
Step four.
Map each requirement to your answer.
Note the volume, section and page where you respond, and the evidence you
attach, such as a certificate, a procedure, a CV or a past project reference.
If you cannot point to an answer, you have found a gap.
For example, a security tender may ask for a use of force policy, licensed
guards and a site security plan.
If your matrix shows a blank next to the use of force policy, you know
exactly what to prepare this week, not on the night before the deadline.
Step five.
Assign an owner and track the status of every row.
Use simple labels: not started, in progress, complete, and reviewed.
Your matrix becomes the control sheet for the whole bid team, and in one
glance you can see what is still open.
Step six.
Before you submit, have someone who did not write the bid check the matrix
against the final documents.
Open every page reference and confirm the answer is really there.
This one check catches most of the errors that cost companies the contract.
Now, the three most common mistakes.
First, starting the matrix too late, after the writing has begun.
Build it on day one, because it shapes the whole response.
Second, writing "noted" or "complied" without evidence.
Evaluators cannot score a promise they cannot see, so always point to the proof.
Third, forgetting the clarifications.
Clients often change a requirement in a clarification letter, and the old
answer is then wrong.
Add every clarification to the matrix the day it arrives.
A few final tips.
Follow the client's own structure and headings.
Answer in the order they ask.
And if the client provides their own compliance form, use theirs, and keep
your matrix as an internal check.
A ready-to-use compliance matrix template, with guidance on every column,
is available at bidandcomply.com.
Templates and guidance for tenders, ISO, security and engineering bids.
Subscribe for more practical bid tips.

metadata.title: How to WIN More Contracts: Responding to RFIs, RFQs & RFPs
metadata.author: ProcuraFind
metadata.shortDescription:
Become a ProcuraFind member today:
https://Procurafind.com

Get Corporate Contract Ready Certified:
https://Procurafind.com/apply

Get the book Be the Contract-Winning Supplier:
https://a.co/d/2YggOdF

Winning corporate and government contracts isn’t just about responding—it’s about responding the right way.

In this video, Dr. Dawn-Nicole McIlwain breaks down how small businesses should approach RFIs, RFQs, and RFPs to significantly increase their chances of winning the work. You’ll learn what procurement teams actually look for, where most businesses go wrong, and how to position your company as a serious, contract-ready supplier.

This training pulls back the curtain on the same principles used inside ProcuraFind to prepare businesses for real corporate opportunities—not theory, but practical strategy.

In this video, you’ll learn:

The difference between RFIs, RFQs, and RFPs—and how each one is evaluated

How to decide which opportunities to pursue (and which to skip)

What procurement teams expect to see in strong responses

Common mistakes that immediately disqualify businesses

How to improve your win rate by responding with clarity, alignment, and confidence

If you’ve ever submitted proposals and heard nothing back—or want to avoid wasting time chasing the wrong opportunities—this video will help you approach RFIs, RFQs, and RFPs with a smarter, more strategic lens.

#rfp #requestforproposal #contracts

metadata.title: RFQ, RFP, and RFI Explained: How to Run a Procurement Bid Process
metadata.author: Intel by CandiMentor
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we break down the crucial differences between RFQ, RFP, and RFI and how to effectively run a procurement bid process. Understanding these concepts can save your organization time and money while ensuring you select the right supplier.
0:00 – A poorly run procurement bid can waste months, inflate costs, and choose the wrong supplier. The dif
0:11 – The Procurement Bid Process
0:21 – Procurement Bid
0:33 – RFI, RFQ, and RFP
0:47 – Choose the Right Document
1:03 – The End-to-End Sequence
1:18 – Three Questions Before Launch
1:31 – RFI: Learn Before Buying
1:42 – RFI
1:56 – What an RFI Reveals
2:07 – Running an RFI
2:20 – RFI Versus RFP
2:33 – RFI in the Real World
2:48 – RFQ: When Price Can Lead
3:00 – RFQ
3:14 – RFQ Essentials
3:26 – Compare the Full Cost
3:39 – Running an RFQ
3:52 – RFQ Versus RFP
4:05 – RFQ Warning Signs
4:19 – RFP: When the Solution Matters
4:31 – RFP
4:43 – Core RFP Components
4:55 – Weighted Evaluation Score
5:09 – Running an RFP
5:25 – Price Versus Value
5:39 – Inside an Evaluation Room
5:54 – Keep the Process Fair
6:10 – From Preferred Bidder to Contract
6:23 – Interview-Ready Takeaways
6:50 – Thank you for watching. Please like and subscribe for more content.
By understanding the differences and applications of RFQ, RFP, and RFI, you can streamline your procurement process and avoid common pitfalls. If you found this video helpful, please like, subscribe, and comment with your thoughts or questions. Let's optimize your procurement strategy together!

#RFQ #RFP #RFI #Procurement #SupplierSelection #BusinessStrategy #Tendering #BiddingProcess #Purchasing #SupplyChain #CostManagement #VendorManagement

segments.text: A poorly run procurement bid can waste
months, inflate costs, and choose the
wrong supplier. The difference between
three short acronyms often decides
whether the purchase succeeds. Every
successful bid starts before a supplier
ever sees a document. First, the buying
team defines the need, the decision
rules, and the path to a contract. A
procurement bid is a controlled way to
invite suppliers into a buying decision.
Instead of choosing informally, the
organization creates a fair process for
collecting and comparing offers. An RFI
is mainly about learning what the market
can provide. An RFQ asks for a defined
price, while an RFP asks suppliers to
design and price a complete response
against stated requirements. Use an RFI
when the team still has questions about
suppliers or available approaches. Move
to an RFQ when the specifications are
clear and price is central and use an
RFP when the solution requires judgment,
design, and tradeoffs. The process
begins with a business requirement, not
with a template. After researching the
market, the buyer issues the appropriate
request, evaluates responses
consistently, and finishes by awarding
the work and formalizing the
relationship. Before launching any bid,
answer three practical questions. What
exactly is needed? Which suppliers
should participate? And how will the
winner be selected? Missing any one of
these creates confusion later. An RFI is
the discovery stage of procurement. It
helps the buyer understand the supplier
landscape before locking in detailed
requirements or asking for binding
prices. Think of an RFI as structured
market research. A company might ask
which capabilities suppliers have, what
implementation models exist, and what
information is needed to design a
realistic purchase. The goal is not to
pick a winner immediately. The buyer is
learning what is possible, how suppliers
normally deliver the work, and where
hidden constraints or cost drivers may
appear. Start by deciding what you need
to learn. Then invite a focused group of
relevant suppliers. Once the responses
are reviewed, use the findings to
sharpen the requirement or decide
whether a formal bid is needed. The RFI
asks, "What could the market offer us?"
The RFP asks, "How would you solve this
defined problem and at what commercial
terms?" That difference in purpose
changes the entire document. Picture a
company exploring a new logistics
platform. Before writing a detailed RFP,
the team speaks with providers to
discover integration options,
implementation timelines, and
capabilities it had not considered. An
RFQ works best when the buyer can
describe the purchase precisely. Because
suppliers are responding to essentially
the same specification, price and
commercial terms become easier to
compare. An RFQ is ideal for
standardized goods, repeat purchases, or
services with measurable specifications.
The buyer already knows what is needed
and mainly wants a competitive,
comparable quote. A strong RFQ removes
ambiguity around quantity, quality,
delivery, and payment. If suppliers
interpret the request differently, the
lowest price may simply reflect a
different scope. The cheapest quoted
unit price is not always the cheapest
purchase. Landed cost adds the expenses
required to get the item delivered and
usable, creating a fairer comparison
between suppliers. Once the
specification is final, suppliers
receive the same information and a clear
deadline. The buyer checks whether each
quote actually complies before comparing
price and negotiating the award. An RFQ
compares suppliers against a known
shopping list. An RFP compares proposed
answers to a business problem. So,
quality, approach, risk, and experience
matter alongside price. RFQS break down
when the specification is vague or
suppliers receive different information.
Also, watch for hidden logistics costs
and quote expiration dates because a low
number may not remain valid through the
decision. An RFP is the most involved of
the three formats. It is designed for
situations where suppliers must propose
an approach, not simply attach a price
to a predefined list. An RFP gives
suppliers a structured problem to solve.
The buyer explains the outcome
constraints and evaluation method, then
compares how each supplier would deliver
the result. A credible RFP tells
suppliers what success looks like and
how responses will be judged. It also
sets the response format and commercial
boundaries so the evaluation stays
consistent. Weighted scoring prevents
one attractive feature from overpowering
the whole decision. For example,
delivery capability might carry more
weight than presentation quality because
it has greater business impact. The RFP
process needs discipline because every
clarification can affect fairness.
Questions are shared consistently.
Proposals are scored against the
published criteria and negotiation
happens after the preferred response is
identified. Price focus is appropriate
when suppliers are offering nearly
identical items. Value focus is better
when a supplier's method, reliability,
or long-term operating cost can
materially change the result. In a
serious RFP evaluation, subject matter
experts score independently before
discussing their results. That simple
separation makes it easier to spot bias,
challenge assumptions, and document why
one proposal ranked higher. Fairness is
not just a legal concern. It improves
the quality of the decision. Give every
bidder the same material information,
separate technical scoring from
commercial review when possible, and
preserve the reasoning behind the award.
Selecting the preferred bidder is not
the finish line. The organization still
needs to verify the supplier, agree on
final terms, obtain approvals, and
prepare the relationship for successful
delivery. For an interview, anchor your
answer to purpose. RFI for discovery,
RFQ for clear specifications and
comparable pricing, and RFP for complex
solutions. Then show that you understand
governance by mentioning criteria,
consistency, and documented decisions.
Once you can match the right document to
the right buying decision, procurement
interviews become far easier. Follow
Candy Mentor for more practical business
skills made clear. Thank you for
watching. Please like and subscribe for
more content.

metadata.title: Government Proposal Writing: Build a Compliance Matrix Step-by-Step
metadata.author: Government Contract Blueprint
metadata.shortDescription:
📊 Take the Government Contract Readiness Scorecard:
https://start.awardarc.app/

Before you start writing a government proposal, build a compliance matrix.

A proposal compliance matrix helps you turn a complicated government solicitation into a structured checklist showing:

What the government requires
Where the requirement appears
Where you'll address it in your proposal
Which evaluation factor may apply
Who owns the response
Whether the requirement is complete

In this beginner-friendly government proposal tutorial, I'll show you how to build a compliance matrix step-by-step and use it to reduce the chances of missing an important RFP requirement.

You'll learn how to track:
Section L proposal instructions
Section M evaluation factors
Statement of Work requirements
Technical requirements
Past performance
Pricing
Required forms and attachments
Proposal ownership
Completion status
Final compliance review

When the Uniform Contract Format is used, Section L provides instructions for preparing proposals and Section M identifies significant evaluation factors and their relative importance.

A compliance matrix is typically a proposal-management tool—not automatically something you submit to the government unless the solicitation requires it.

📊 Find out how ready your business is:
https://start.awardarc.app/

Subscribe for beginner-friendly government contracting tutorials covering SAM.gov, solicitations, government proposal writing, capability statements, bidding strategies, and AI-powered GovCon workflows.

#GovernmentProposal #GovernmentContracts #GovernmentContracting #GovCon #RFP

**Turn 40-hour RFP responses into 4-hour wins using AI.** In this exclusive workshop, I reveal my complete AI workflow for responding to Government of Canada RFPs. ✅ **Winning AI prompts** – Copy my exact templates for ChatGPT and Claude  
✅ **Professional proposal generation** – Get publication-ready drafts with proper methodology, team quals, and risk mitigation

metadata.title: 3 Smart Ways to Fund Your Government Contract *Credit Cards, Factoring, & Purchase Orders*
metadata.author: Debra Smith
metadata.shortDescription:
Winning a government contract is exciting — but how do you cover the upfront costs before the government pays you? In this video, I break down three powerful funding options that can help small businesses bridge the cash flow gap: credit card funding, factoring companies, and purchase order financing.

You’ll learn:
✅ Why each option is a great fit for different types of contracts
✅ How to decide which funding method works best for your business
✅ Tips to use these tools strategically without getting stuck in debt

Whether you’re just starting in government contracting or scaling up to larger awards, this video will give you the clarity and confidence to fund your contracts the smart way.

metadata.title: Ep. 2: Wide Area Workflow (WAWF) Explained | How to Invoice with the DoD & Avoid Rejections
metadata.author: Acquisition Pro Tips
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to Episode 2 of Acquisition Pro Tips! In this video, I cover Wide Area Workflow (WAWF) — the Department of Defense’s secure electronic invoicing system. Whether you’re a vendor, contracting officer, or government resource advisor, this walkthrough covers important facts you need to know to get invoices submitted, accepted, and paid on time.

#governmentcontracting #governmentemployee #governmentofficial #contracting #federalcontracts  

Here’s what we’ll cover in today’s video:
~WAWF basics and why it exists
~The importance of CAGE and NCAGE codes (U.S. vs NATO/foreign vendors)
~WAWF roles: vendors, inspectors, acceptors, contracting officers, resource advisors, and DFAS
~How Contracting Officers must complete the WAWF Payment Instructions clause (DFARS 252.232-7006)
~Invoice document types (Combo, 2-in-1, Cost Vouchers, Progress & Performance-Based Payments, Fast Pay)
~UID requirements in WAWF and how to avoid rejections
~Foreign vendor invoicing process
~Prompt Payment Act deadlines and interest penalties
~Common mistakes vendors make and how to avoid them
~GAO lessons learned & insights from Forman’s article Better Late Than Never?

Chapters
0:00 Intro
2:29 CAGE & NCAGE Codes
3:00 WAWF Roles
5:04 Invoice Document Types
7:51 Common Invoicing Mistakes
10:48 Acquisition Pro Tips

References mentioned in this episode of Acquisition Pro Tips:
~FAR Prompt Payment Clause
https://www.acquisition.gov/far/52.232-25
~DFARS WAWF Payment Instructions Clause
https://www.acquisition.gov/dfars/252.232-7006
~Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS) – WAWF Information
https://www.dfas.mil/contractorsvendors/wideareaworkflow/
~Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment (PIEE) Portal
https://piee.eb.mil
~Foreign Vendor Support Guide (PIEE)
https://pieetraining.eb.mil/wbt/wawf/documents/Foreign_Vendor_Support.pdf
~WAWF Vendor Training Resources (PIEE)
https://pieetraining.eb.mil/wbt/xhtml/wbt/wawf/index.xhtml
~GAO Report – Contract Financing and Payments (2024)
https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-105106
~Forman, D. R. (2024, Feb 26). Better Late Than Never
https://www.federalnewsnetwork.com/acquisition-policy/2024/02/better-late-than-never/

If you find this helpful, don’t forget to like, subscribe, and hit the notification bell so you never miss another Acquisition Pro Tip.

⚖️ Disclaimer
The views and opinions expressed on this channel are my own and do not represent the official position of the United States Air Force, the Department of Defense, or any other federal agency. This content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice.

Welcome to Acquisition Pro Tips, where
we seek to demystify and break down the
essentials of government contracting so
you can navigate the process with
confidence. I'm Josh, a warranted
government contracting officer, and
today we're diving into wide area
workflow, better known as WAFT. Let's
get started.
Traditionally, the DoD acquisition
process was paperbased and labor
intensive. Invoices, receiving reports,
and payments were mailed or even handd
delivered, which led to delays, lost
documents, and interest penalties under
the Prompt Payment Act.
To fix this, the DoD launched the
paperless contracting initiative in the
late 1990s. And by 1999, WATF became
operational. WATF creates a virtual
folder combining the three critical
documents needed for payment. The
contract, the invoice, and the receiving
report. The system is web- based,
secure, uses digital signatures, and
ensures documents are tracked at every
step. Benefits include global
accessibility,
fewer errors, faster processing, and
fewer prompt payment act violations.
What used to take weeks can now take
days, sometimes just minutes.
So, what is WAT? The WATH application,
now part of the procurement integrated
enterprise environment, also known as
PI, is the official DoD's system for
electronic invoicing, receipt,
acceptance, and property transfer.
Vendors can submit invoices directly.
Government officials can inspect and
accept online, and DEFAS can process
payments securely. Notifications are
automatically sent by email and all
required supporting documents are stored
in one place.
This not only streamlines the process,
it protects taxpayers by reducing
interest penalties and ensures vendors
are paid on time. But before you can
even log into WAFT, your company must be
registered in SAM.gov with a valid code.
US vendors require a cage code. Foreign
vendors in NATO countries require an end
cage code which is internationally
assigned. If you haven't seen my first
video, go check it out. I explain step
by step how to get your cage or end cage
code. Without it, WAT won't recognize
you. So, now let's go over some of the
roles you might find in WT. Different
players share responsibilities in WAFT.
Vendors submit invoices, check status,
and fix rejections. Inspectors verify
quality of goods or services. Acceptors
confirm receipt on behalf of the
government. Resource advisers ensure
funds are available. Pay officials, also
known as DEFAS, authorize and issue
payment while contracting officers
ensure the contract has accurate WAFT
payment instructions.
If one link breaks, the entire chain
stalls. Now, I want to speak directly to
my fellow contracting officers, more
specifically regarding the WAT payment
instructions clause, which is in DARce.
It must be filled in completely and
accurately. And here's how. Document
type. In this section, enter combo for
supply contracts. And in this section,
enter twoin one for services.
Use cost voucher progress payment or
performancebased payment if that's what
the contract requires. Routing data
table. Fill in contract DODAX pay office
issue by admin inspect ship to for
supplies and commodities service
approver and service acceptor for
service type contracts.
Inspection and acceptance specifically
source or destination as outlined in the
contract. Validate DODAX. Confirm that
each DOAC that you list has active users
in WAFT for that role. If you get this
wrong, vendors cannot bill correctly and
payment delays are almost guaranteed.
GAO has sustained multiple protests due
to unclear instructions. So, make sure
your clause is airtight. Now, on to
invoice document types.
Submitting the wrong invoice type is the
fastest way to get rejected. Here's what
to know. The combo, most common for
supplies, combines invoice and receiving
reports.
Two in one for services where invoice
and receiving reports go together.
Commercial invoice used with fast pay
when allowed by the contract. Cost
vouchers for cost reimbursement and
labor hour contracts. Progress payments
based on incurred costs, 80% for large
businesses and 95% for small businesses.
Performance-based payments are based on
milestones up to 90% of the contract
value. This is the government's
preferred method of financing.
Important though, progress and
performance payments cannot both be used
on the same contract. Here is some
information for my foreign vendors. For
non US vendors, invoicing requires extra
setup. First, request that your endage
code be added to the PI foreign vendor
group through the help desk. Then, your
company's contractor administrator or
CAM must register your code, input
banking information, and activate
access. Only then can you invoice like a
US vendor. If you need the step-by-step
guide, the foreign vendor support PDF is
linked in the video description. Another
common requirement is the UID, unique
item identification. Certain items,
usually over $5,000 or specified in the
contract, must be marked with a unique
code and entered into WATH. Vendors must
physically mark items, enter UID data
correctly in the invoice, and use the
WAT UID wizard to avoid mistakes. The
government's role is to make UID
requirements clear in the contract and
to validate quickly. Missing UID entries
will get your invoice rejected. Prompt
payment and interest penalties. The
prompt payment clause requires payment
within 30 days of receiving a proper
invoice. If the government is late,
interest is automatically added by
DEFAS. The US Treasury updates the rate
twice per year. For example, right now
But remember, the clock only starts when
a proper invoice is submitted. If your
invoice is missing details or is
incorrect, interest won't apply. All
payment instruction links and treasury
rate updates are listed in my
description. So, here are a few common
mistakes and how to avoid them. This is
my top 10 list on why your invoices will
get rejected. Number one, contract data
mismatch. Copy straight from the
contract and not from memory. Number
two, wrong DOAC. Double check against
WAFT instructions. Number three, missing
attachments. include DD250s, time
sheets, or required docs. Number four,
wrong invoice type, combo versus
twoinone, etc. Number five, quantity
price errors. Ensure line items match
exactly. Number six, acceptance delays.
Coordinate with your acceptor early.
Number seven, wrong payoff routing. Use
the correct DEFAS code. Number eight,
typing errors. Even one digit wrong can
derail you. Number nine, missing
certifications mark. Final invoice when
applicable. Number 10, submitting at the
wrong time. Too early or too late, both
cause problems. Think of it this way.
Measure twice, invoice once. Now, let's
talk about fast pay. If your contract
has the fast pay clause, you can be paid
before acceptance, but your invoice must
be marked fast pay or it will process
like a normal one. Remember, fast pay
does not wave inspection or acceptance.
It just shifts when the payment is
released. WATF notifications. Every
action in WATF generates an automatic
email. These go to organizational
inboxes, not personal addresses. Make
sure your organization routes these
emails properly. Otherwise, invoices can
sit unworked for weeks without anyone
realizing it. Now, let's talk about the
benefits of My Invoice tool. Do you want
to know if DFAS paid you? Use the My
Invoice tool. It lets vendors check
invoice status, see payment schedules,
and verify if interest was included.
Don't wait until you think something's
wrong. Monitor proactively. The GAO has
made it clear both sides, vendors and
government are responsible for invoicing
accuracy. Bad instructions or sloppy
invoices create disputes. In David
Foreman's 2024 article, Better late Than
Never, he highlighted GAO sustained
decisions where agencies try to fix
records after the fact. GAO rejected
those excuses, stressing that accuracy
and documentation must happen upfront.
The lesson is simple. Do it right the
first time. So, let's wrap this video up
with a few acquisition pro tips. Here
are your pro tips for WAFT success.
Number one, get a valid cage code or end
cage code before you start. Number two,
match invoice type to the contract every
time. Number three, contracting
officers, fill in WAFT instructions
fully and accurately. Number four, for
vendors, validate before submitting and
mark final invoice when applicable.
Number five, for resource advisors,
approve quickly and give detailed
feedback. Number six, for foreign
vendors, coordinate early with the PI
help desk. Number seven, monitor WAFT
email alerts in my invoice for statuses.
Number eight, use the UID wizard if
required. Number nine, FastPay, don't
forget to label it. And number 10, and
above all, communicate. A twominute
email can save 30 days of delay. And
that's episode two of acquisition pro
tips. WATH may look complicated, but
once you understand the roles, document
types, and common pitfalls, it becomes a
straightforward tool. All useful web
links, training guides, and payment
resources I've mentioned today are
listed in the description down below. In
our next episode, we'll shift focus to
government mission partners and
customers, and I'll show you how to
build a better requirements package that
sets contracts up for success from day
one. If you found this video helpful,
don't forget to like, subscribe, and hit
the bell so you never miss another
acquisition pro tip.
[Music]
Honey,
make sure
we can celebrate.

metadata.title: Ep. 9: How to Submit a WAWF COMBO Invoice | Vendor Step-by-Step Tutorial
metadata.author: Acquisition Pro Tips
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode 9 focuses on vendor education — guiding suppliers, contractors, and small businesses through the invoicing process in the Department of Defense’s Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment (PIEE). From creating your first invoice to interpreting DFARS payment clauses, this training demystifies government invoicing and helps vendors get paid faster.

#governmentcontracting #governmentemployee #governmentofficial #contracting #federalcontracts  

Chapters
00:00 Intro
01:53 The Vendor Quick Kit
03:00 PIEE Access & The Vendor Role
04:17 Reading the WAWF Clause
05:21 Submission Methods
06:26 CREATING THE COMBO IN WAWF
10:56 WAWF Messages & Errors
12:00 CAGE Codes
12:45 Foreign Vendors
13:26 Contract Clause & References
14:34 The Final Steps
15:57 Conclusion

⚠️ Disclaimer:
The views and opinions expressed in this video are solely those of the creator and do not represent the official policy or position of the Department of Defense, the U.S. Air Force, or any government agency. All examples, data, and contract information are fictional and used for educational purposes only.

🎵 Music Credit:
“Eat Your Young” by Hozier – used under license / fair use for theme reference.
Additional background music licensed through Envato Elements.

📌 Helpful Links:
📄 PIEE Portal – https://piee.eb.mil

📘 DFARS 252.232-7006 – https://www.acquisition.gov/dfars

📚 WAWF Vendor Training – https://pieetraining.eb.mil

Before we even start building the invoice, let's talk about the three ways vendors can send documents into WAT. First, there's the interactive web application, the version we'll use in this video. It's perfect for small businesses or vendors with low volume. Just don't let it sit idle too long. It times out after 15 minutes of inactivity. Second, there's SFTTP, secure file transfer protocol. This is great for companies that submit lots of invoices or have big data batches to upload automatically. And third, there's EDI or electronic data interchange, which connects directly with the global exchange service. That's for vendors who integrate WAT with their own systems. Acquisition pro tip number four, [music] use the method that matches your business needs. For occasional invoicing, the web version is simple and reliable, but if you submit dozens a week, talk to your IT team about SFTTP or EDI. Automation saves sanity. Section five, creating a combo in WAT. Now, we're ready to build the combo. I'll follow the official WAFT training slides so you can see what the system looks like, but I'll use our Sino mobile contract so it all makes sense in context. Once you're in WAFT, go to vendor and click create document. The first thing you'll see is a request for your cage code, contract number, and order number. Select the appropriate cage. Enter your contract number and your order number if applicable. If you're wondering where to find those, check the first page of your contract. On a DD155, that's blocks 9, [music] 1, and 2. On a SF1449, blocks 17 alpha, 2, and [music] 4. On an SF26, blocks 7, 2, and 4. And on an SF33, [music] blocks 15 alpha 2 and 6. In our example, we're using an SF1449. So those blocks are right up top. Once those are in, click next. The next screen shows your pay official DOAC which for us is F87700. That's the defense finance and accounting services DODAC or DEFAS. This office pays the invoice. Below that, choose invoice and receiving report combo as your document type. Then we'll move to the routing codes. From the waft clause in our contract, we'll input issue by FA1234, administered by the same DOAC, inspect by SS 001, and ship to, you guessed it, [music] the same DODAC. These codes ensure your invoice travels to the right reviewers. [music] Next, we'll confirm the header tab. For SCO mobile's example, shipment number fo ne03, shipment date, invoice number, sinko 901, invoice date, today's date, and final shipment marked yes because this will be the one and only invoice under [music] this contract. The shipment and invoice number are your company's specific and internal numbers and will not be found on the contract because they are generated by you, the vendor. Scroll down to the transportation data section. Here we'll enter our transportation account code or TAC. And for this example, we're making up one. So here we're going to put delta 9 x-ray 6 and our transportation control number or TCN which is typically a 17digit long code provided to you by the government. The TCN uniquely identifies this shipment which in this example weighs 90 lb. Both the TAC and TCN are typically found in the inspection and acceptance section of the contract. If your contract doesn't include a TAC or TCN, check submit transportation data later, but remember to update it before payment. Not all contracts are going to use a TAC or TCN, and is typically done when using a state side DLA consolidation point. Now, on to the line item tab. Each contract line item or CLIN becomes its own entry here. For CLIN one, enter product or service ID. metadata.title: Federal Contracting Strategy: HUBZone vs Every Other SBA Cert
metadata.author: Squared Compass
metadata.shortDescription:
Is HUBZone Certification Worth It? What the Federal Contracting Data Really Says

Thinking about HUBZone certification? In this video, we break down what HUBZone is, how set-asides work, the gap between federal goals vs. actual awards, and when HUBZone makes sense versus 8(a), WOSB/EDWOSB, and SDVOSB. You’ll get a practical, data-driven verdict plus the maintenance requirements people overlook, so you can decide if the juice is worth the squeeze.

What you’ll learn (quick hits):

What HUBZone certification is and who qualifies

The 3% federal goal vs. real award outcomes, and what that means for you

Pros & cons of HUBZone (and hidden maintenance costs)

HUBZone vs 8(a), WOSB/EDWOSB, SDVOSB, which is more strategic for your situation

When to pursue HUBZone, and when to focus elsewhere

TL;DR: HUBZone can work, but it’s not one-size-fits-all. If it’s the only certification you can realistically obtain, it may be worth it. If you can qualify for other programs with stronger pipelines, your win rate may be higher there. The video explains how to decide, step-by-step.

Chapters

00:00 Intro & What We’ll Cover
00:45 What Is HUBZone? Eligibility & Basics
02:10 Goals vs. Reality: Understanding HUBZone Award Results
04:05 Pros, Cons & Real Costs of Maintenance
06:30 Should You Apply? A Simple Decision Framework
08:15 HUBZone vs 8(a), WOSB/EDWOSB & SDVOSB (Comparative View)
10:05 Agency Behavior & Practical Targeting Tips
11:30 Final Verdict: When HUBZone Helps (and When It Doesn’t)
12:10 Resources & Next Steps

Who this video is for

Small businesses exploring SBA certifications

Owners weighing HUBZone vs 8(a)/WOSB/SDVOSB

New vendors in federal contracting and government set-asides

Capture/BD teams building a certifications strategy

FAQs (for fast answers & indexing)

Is HUBZone certification worth it in 2024?
It depends on your pipeline, location eligibility, and whether HUBZone is your only practical path to a set-aside advantage. The video shows how to decide using goals, award trends, and maintenance effort.

Which is better: HUBZone or 8(a)/WOSB/EDWOSB/SDVOSB?
No single “winner.” It’s about fit, customer demand, your past performance, and where your target agencies actually award work. We compare trade-offs so you can choose strategically.

What are the hidden costs or risks of HUBZone?
Ongoing principal office and employee residency requirements can be challenging. We cover the maintenance checklist so you’re not surprised later.

Can I stack certifications?
Yes. Stacking (e.g., HUBZone + WOSB) can expand opportunity sets, but prioritize what your target agencies use most.

Resources Mentioned

SBA HUBZone Program (eligibility, maps, guidance)

SBA 8(a), WOSB/EDWOSB, SDVOSB program pages

Recent federal small business goals vs. award summaries

Agency forecasts & past performance tools

Work with us / Next steps

If you want help deciding whether to pursue HUBZone, or to map certifications to real contract opportunities, drop “HUBZone” in the comments and tell us your NAICS + target agencies. We’ll point you to the most relevant next steps.

Keywords (help the algorithm understand the video):
HUBZone certification, is HUBZone worth it, HUBZone vs 8(a), HUBZone vs WOSB, HUBZone vs SDVOSB, SBA certifications, government set-asides, federal contracting for small business, small business set asides, how to get HUBZone certified, HUBZone maintenance requirements, HUBZone goals vs reality, should I apply for HUBZone, federal contracting strategy, government contracting tips

Hashtags: #HUBZone #GovernmentContracting #SmallBusiness #SBA #SetAsides

Granted, agencies who do not meet their hub zone goals are incentivized to do business with a hub zone certified company. However, from the data, these agencies aren't putting out the number of hub zone set aside solicitations that would support this. Housing and urban development was at 0.24%. Overall governmentwide, every single agency in the government for hub zone set aside certifications spent 0.44%. So is hub zone certification worth it? For many companies, the answer is no. Between the lack of solicitations targeted at a and awarded to hub zone companies as well as the requirements to obtain and maintain hub zone status, the juice just isn't worth the squeeze. However, and here's the catch, if hub zone certification is the only business set aside certification that you can obtain, minus the standard small business set aside certification, which every small business has, then going after the hub zone certification, could be your way into winning more contracts and growing your revenue. metadata.title: Government Contracting Certifications for Beginners: WOSB, SDVOSB, 8(a) & HUBZone
metadata.author: Nick Waters GovCon
metadata.shortDescription:
Which federal small business certification should you pursue? In this video, I break down WOSB, SDVOSB, 8(a), and HUBZone so you can understand who each program is for, what opportunities it can open, and which one may fit your business.

We’ll look at the key qualifications, the contracting benefits, and what to check before you apply. You may qualify for more than one program.

Check your eligibility with SBA: https://certifications.sba.gov/

Which certification are you considering? Let me know in the comments.

Subscribe for practical, step-by-step government contracting guidance.

#GovernmentContracting #WOSB #SDVOSB #8aCertification #HUBZone #WOSB #SDVOSB #HUBZone #8aCertification #FederalContracting #GovernmentContracts #SmallBusinessCertifications #WomenOwnedBusiness #VeteranOwnedBusiness #GovCon

metadata.title: Intro to the 4 Small Business Programs in Federal Contracting | WOSB, SDVOSB, 8(a), HUBZone
metadata.author: Neil McDonnell
metadata.shortDescription:
Introduction to the 4 Small Business Programs in Federal Contracting | WOSB, SDVOSB, 8(a), HUBZone  
In this training video,  @neilmcdonnell of the GovCon Chamber of Commerce introduces several SBA programs that help small businesses win federal contracts.  Programs are available for–
Women-Owned Small Businesses; Service-disabled Veteran-Owned Small Businesses;  HUBZone located businesses; 8(a) Business Development program

5% Contracting dollar award goal
Women-owned small business
Small disadvantaged business

3% Contracting dollar award goal
Service-disabled veteran-owned small business
Small business in a HUBZone

Participating in these programs helps small businesses:
• Win a fair share of federal contracts
• Qualify for exclusive set-aside and sole-source contracts
• Partner with established contractors to win contracts
• Get business mentoring and education to learn how federal contracting works

FIND OUT MORE
SBA Contracting assistance programs 
– https://www.sba.gov/federal-contracting/contracting-assistance-programs

👉  Neil McDonnell provides FREE federal sales and Business Development training every day live 12N EST on YouTube and LinkedIn.  Join our government contracting trainings community. 
• https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/2023-federal-sales-training-neil-mcdonnell/  👈 
------------------------------
🔥   “Government Contracting is not a Secret... it’s just a process.” Neil McDonnell

✅  NEWS FROM NEIL MCDONNELL – 
👉 "Become the Federal Business Developer that Companies Want in 2023!'
After 250+ daily LinkedIn live training sessions, Neil has designed a 2023 version of his BD course to teach you how to become a highly successful BD professional. Get the knowledge and confidence to identify opportunities and build relationships that lead to federal revenue.

👉 GO TO  https://www.neilmcdonnell.com/

👉 Once you complete this course, you will have the knowledge, skills and confidence to –
➡️. Balance a successful career with a remote lifestyle (flexibility!)
➡️. Apply your highly transferable BD skills to any company (competence!)
➡️. Find financial security in a predictable, recession-proof marketplace (stability!) 
___________
✅  HOST and Your Guide to Government Contracting   | Neil McDonnell, President of GovCon Chamber of Commerce and author of "SPIN Selling for Government Contracting"
#experiencematters 

A leading Federal Sales expert with 20+ years as technology small business owner and federal contractor, Neil has personally won and supported multi-million dollar contracts for Defense and Civilian agencies including:
➡️   US Army, US Navy, and US Air Force
➡️   Executive Office of the White House
➡️   Departments of Education, Transportation, Interior and Energy
➡️   Veterans Affairs and HHS and 
➡️   Large Prime contractors including Booz Allen and GDIT

As president of the GovCon Chamber of Commerce, Neil  has:
➡️   Trained 1000s of small business owners and business developers since 2018
➡️   Created the 7-Step Process for Federal Revenue Success

The government's goal federally is to try to um and they achieve this every year, get 23% set aside to small businesses as prime contractors. They have subcategories in that 23%. metadata.title: Does the #sdvosb Certification Help Win Government Contracts?
metadata.author: GovClose | DoD Contract Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Does the SDVOSB certification actually help a small business?

In this live training, I’ll show you exactly how to find out which federal agencies truly prioritize SDVOSBs—and which ones are wasting your time.

Here’s what we’re covering:

How much money is really being awarded to SDVOSBs right now

Which agencies are consistently using SDVOSB set-asides to award contracts

A repeatable, step-by-step method to identify the best agency targets for your business

If you're SDVOSB-certified and serious about winning contracts, this training will help you stop chasing dead-end opportunities and start building a focused, high-value pipeline.

We’ll also take a closer look at the Department of Veterans Affairs—what they get right, where they fall short, and how to approach them the right way.

This session is ideal for:
SDVOSBs, HUBZone companies, 8(a), WOSBs, and any small business ready to stop guessing and start winning.

Bonus: I’ll also show you how we use this same process inside the GovClose Certification Program to help students build real pipelines, land meetings, and win.

About Me
I’m Richard C. Howard, Lt Col (Ret), former U.S. Air Force acquisitions officer. I managed over $82 billion in federal contracts and now help businesses across the country win in the public sector through GovClose.

If you’re looking for the truth about federal contracting—and you’re tired of the fluff—this is for you.

Government contracting isn’t about who you know. It’s about having a real strategy.

JOIN the GovClose Community  
RING the bell 🔔 on my LinkedIn profile for real-world GovCon insights  
👉(https://www.linkedin.com/in/govclose/)

metadata.title: How to Fight the SBA: Stop Collections on Your EIDL Loan
metadata.author: Keck Legal, LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Did you receive a notice from the SBA or a collection agency about your EIDL loan? Don't ignore it. In 2026, the federal government has ramped up enforcement, and "scary letters" in the mail are often the final warning before your debt is referred to the U.S. Treasury.

In this video, we break down why SBA EIDL debt is fundamentally different from tax debt and what business owners in Atlanta, Alpharetta, and throughout Georgia need to know to protect their livelihoods. We discuss:

The Default Timeline: What it means when a collection agency gets involved.

SBA vs. Treasury: Why you must act before the Treasury Offset Program (TOP) begins seizing tax refunds or garnishing wages without a court order.

Renegotiation Options: How to pursue Hardship Accommodation Plans or an Offer in Compromise (OIC).

The Power of Chapter 11: Why a court-approved reorganization can force a repayment plan even if the SBA refuses to negotiate.

Personal Guarantees: Are you personally on the hook for your business loan?

Every business situation is unique. Whether you are dealing with a $20,000 loan or a $2M personally guaranteed debt, the strategy changes. Watch to understand your rights under Georgia law and the Northern District of Georgia bankruptcy guidelines.

Take control of your business debt today.

Book a consultation with our Atlanta legal team: https://kecklegal.com

metadata.title: SBA Franchise Directory 2026: Is Your Franchise on the SBA List?
metadata.author: The Money Rules
metadata.shortDescription:
Getting an SBA loan for a franchise in 2026 starts with one list: the SBA Franchise Directory. Since the SBA brought it back in June 2025 (and kept it in the rules that took effect October 1, 2026), a brand that counts as a franchise must be on it, or a lender can't approve the loan. Being listed is not an endorsement. We cover what counts as a franchise, how brands get listed, the 10% start-up equity rule (and how prepaid costs can count), and a full worked example: a $400,000 franchise, a $360,000 SBA 7(a) loan, the 10% maximum rate (prime 7% + 3%), about $4,757 a month, and the $8,100 FY2027 guarantee fee. Then the odd rate-cap step that can make a smaller loan cost more, the 1.15 cash-flow test, the three FDD Items to read (7, 19 and 20), the FTC's 14-day rule, the 2026 citizenship rule, and viewer questions on buying an existing business.

Rates are SBA maximums as of November 2026, not quotes; your lender can charge less.

Sources:
- SBA Franchise Directory (file effective October 28, 2026): https://legacy.sba.gov/document/support-sba-franchise-directory
- SBA business guide: SBA Franchise Directory: https://legacy.sba.gov/business-guide/plan-your-business/buy-existing-business-or-franchise/sba-franchise-directory
- SBA SOP 50 10 8.1 (effective October 1, 2026): https://legacy.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs
- CRS Insight IN12549: Changes to SBA Business Loan Program Policies in Early 2025: https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2025-04-28_IN12549_747ba3619ab620f87ababdaf70278efb869b7f49.html
- SBA Information Notice 5000-881797: 7(a) Fees for Fiscal Year 2027: https://legacy.sba.gov/document/information-notice-5000-881797-fy-2027-7a-program-fees
- Federal Reserve H.15 Selected Interest Rates: https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h15/
- SBA Policy Notice 5000-876441: Citizenship and Residency Requirements (effective March 1, 2026): https://legacy.sba.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/Policy%20Notice%205000-876441%20-%20Update%20to%20Citizenship%20and%20Residency%20Requirements%20and%20Recission%20of%20PN%2050000-872050.pdf
- FTC Franchise Rule, 16 CFR 436.1 (definition of a franchise), via Cornell LII: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/436.1
- FTC Franchise Rule, 16 CFR 436.2 (14-day and 7-day rules), via Cornell LII: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/436.2
- FTC Franchise Rule, 16 CFR 436.5 (the 23 disclosure Items), via Cornell LII: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/436.5
- 13 CFR 121.301 (affiliation for SBA business loans), via Cornell LII: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/13/121.301
- SBA Microloans: https://www.sba.gov/funding-programs/loans/microloans

The $400,000 franchise is an illustration, not a real brand. Talk to your lender, a franchise attorney and your tax pro about your own situation.

General information, not personalized advice.

And if you scroll further down, you'll see even more information about this contract. You'll see a description, so you know you're looking at the right contract. And you'll even see the number of bids they received on the contract. So now we know that the current contract, which goes from March 2020 through September 2024, has a value of $47,352. Now you might think you're done, but there's one more important step and that's finding the scope of work for the current contract. Now why is that? Because the work might have changed since the last time the contract was bid. For instance, the current contract might be for two people, but going forward the government needs 10 people. Work scope sometimes changes and these changes could drastically affect the price you bid. In our example, we want to see what work scope they were bidding on when they bid $47,352. To find this, we're going to go back into SAM to find the old solicitation and review its work scope. Here at SAM.gov, click on Search and then Select Domain and then Contract Opportunities. Now in this Keyword Search box, I'm going to click on Exact Phrase and then enter the phrase I want to search for. I'm going to search for Seeley Lake, and I'm also going to search for janitorial. This will give me a list of contracts that contain both the words Seeley Lake and also the word janitorial. The results are here on the right and we're only seeing the current solicitation because we need to do one more thing. We scroll down to the bottom of the filter list where it says Status, and we need to change the status from Active to Inactive because we're searching for an old solicitation. And now we see a list of 12 contracts that match our search criteria. Note that on this first result, the contract offers, the bids, were due on February 13th, 2020. So that looks like the contract we're looking for. The other 11 results are all older contracts. So let's click on the name for the first result to see its details. And then when we scroll down, we see a link to download the solicitation. That's this document here. So now we know the current contractor bid $47,000 and we can read the solicitation to see the work scope that they based that price on. And there you have it. You now know how to find out what the government is currently paying for the work you want to bid on. So go ahead and add finding the current contract to your bidding workflow. And if you're having trouble finding the predecessor contract, it's also okay to ask the government directly. Every solicitation includes an email address where you can submit questions directly to the government. We went through this fast, and we've only scratched the surface on what FPDS can do for you. You can use it to find who's buying, what they're buying, how much they're buying, how often they're buying. So for the next step in how to use information to gain a real competitive advantage and win more contracts, watch my complete FPDS tutorial next. It's a detailed guide that walks you through how to find buyers, research competitors, find potential teaming partners, and uncover data that's going to give you a real advantage in your bids. So go ahead, click on that video and take the next step. Thanks for watching and I'll see you in the next video.

metadata.title: How to Find WOSB Set Asides Using FPDS | Government Contracting
metadata.author: Neil McDonnell
metadata.shortDescription:
Find Woman Owned Small Business Set Asides Using FPDS | Government Contracting. One of the best ways to find opportunities that will be a fit for your company is to look at 'expiring' contracts using FPDS.
Doing so allows you to find ones that really fit what you offer and have a great chance of being funded.

In this training, I'll teach you how to:
• Use FPDS to search for WOSB opportunities that match your services
• How to find additional information about each opportunity before it's released by the contracting shop
• How to start pursuing each opportunity that's a fit for you

✅  Visit our dedicated series for women-owned small businesses.  https://www.govconchamber.com/wosb

👉  Neil McDonnell provides FREE federal sales and Business Development training every day live 12N EST on YouTube and LinkedIn.  Join our government contracting trainings community. 
• https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/2023-federal-sales-training-neil-mcdonnell/  👈 
------------------------------
🔥   “Government Contracting is not a Secret... it’s just a process.” Neil McDonnell

👉 "Become the Federal Business Developer that Companies Want in 2023!'
After 200+ daily LinkedIn live training sessions, Neil is designing a 2023 version of his BD course to teach you how to become a highly successful BD professional. Get the knowledge and confidence to identify opportunities and build relationships that lead to federal revenue.

👉 GO TO:  NeilMcDonnell.com for more information and to be notified when the training is released. https://www.neilmcdonnell.com/

👉 Once you complete this course, you will have the knowledge, skills and confidence to –
➡️. Balance a successful career with a remote lifestyle (flexibility!)
➡️. Apply your highly transferable BD skills to any company (competence!)
➡️. Find financial security in a predictable, recession-proof marketplace (stability!) 
___________
✅  HOST and Your Guide to Government Contracting   | Neil McDonnell, President of GovCon Chamber of Commerce and author of "SPIN Selling for Government Contracting"
#experiencematters 

A leading Federal Sales expert with 20+ years as technology small business owner and federal contractor, Neil has personally won and supported multi-million dollar contracts for Defense and Civilian agencies including:
➡️   US Army, US Navy, and US Air Force
➡️   Executive Office of the White House
➡️   Departments of Education, Transportation, Interior and Energy
➡️   Veterans Affairs and HHS and

As president of the GovCon Chamber of Commerce, Neil  has:

➡️   Created the 7-Step Process for Federal Revenue Success
➡️   Hosted 250+ daily LinkedIn live federal sales trainings

metadata.title: Mastering FAR Part 12: The Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO)
metadata.author: ASI Education
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn more about ASI Education PRO
     - https://educationpro.asigovernment.com/


Buying commercial items is the "favorite child" of acquisition reform, yet somehow, the process always seems to get complicated. In this quick video, we’re unpacking FAR Part 12 and exploring how the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO) has fundamentally shifted the landscape of government contracting.

We cover the major consolidation of simplified acquisition procedures, the relocation of commercial terms from Part 13 to Part 12, and how the new $9M threshold changes your day-to-day procurement strategy.

What You’ll Learn:
Commercial Construction: Why FAR 2.101 now clarifies that commercial services include construction and how that impacts Part 36.

The $9M Shift: Understanding 12.201-1 and the new RFQ-to-PO lane for acquisitions under $9M.

Part 8 vs. Part 12: When to use Best-In-Class (BIC) vehicles and GSA schedules over standalone Part 12 procedures.

Innovative Evaluation: How Comparative Evaluations and Contracting Officer’s Discretion replace rigid, traditional scoring systems.

Business Judgment: Why the "late is late" rule for bid submissions no longer applies under 12.203(c)(1).

Clause Reduction: The elimination of 52.212-3 and 52.212-5, resulting in a 30% reduction in contract clauses.

The RFO is all about streamlining, innovation, and empowering Contracting Officers to use their best business judgment. Whether you're a seasoned CO or a vendor looking to understand the new rules of the road, this video breaks down the most impactful changes in the FAR today.

Want the full RFO series?
This is just one part of our comprehensive breakdown of the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul. To access every module and earn CLPs, join the community at ASI Education Pro.

Don’t forget to Like, Subscribe, and hit the Bell for more updates on Federal Acquisition and FAR updates!

FAR Part 12 explained for small businesses: Sell Commercial Products Without Assuming the Rules Disappear.

Ellen Beebe's background is in estimating and pricing. She spent 33 years at different levels of estimating and pricing and has a full understanding of FAR Part 15 and FAR Part 12.

Inside the FAR, where the definitions are in the Federal Acquisition Regulation, it describes what a commercial item is versus what's not commercial. And you can only sell commercial items under FAR Part 12. The Raytheon experience, while we had some commercial items that we sold under FAR Part 12, we are mostly under FAR part 15, either competitive or sole-source.

FAR Part 15 is utilized by the federal government for competitive as well as sole-source proposals. If you are a sole source and you are putting a proposal together that's over $2 million, then you fall under FAR Part 15 table 15.2 and that is a description of how you build certified cost or pricing data for a proposal. Table 15.2 is very descriptive, you have to build a bill of materials, you have to consolidate that bill of materials across all the line items, as well as provide support for all the estimates in the cost.

Of course, if it is a commercial item, you have to prove commerciality as part of the proposal process. So you'll need to be able to show that it's been sold to the general public in some way, shape or form. Generally that's by providing invoices to the buying command.

metadata.title: FAR Part 47 (Simplified) | Align Delivery, Freight, and Risk Before Shipment
metadata.author: Win Government Contracts with GovSuccess
metadata.shortDescription:
The equipment price is only part of the delivery decision. FAR Part 47 addresses transportation acquisitions and the shipping terms used in supply contracts, including responsibilities that can change the delivered cost.

In this GovSuccess lesson:
• Identify the transaction and delivery point
• Separate freight charges from risk and acceptance
• Check routing and carrier restrictions
• Hypothetical example and practical contractor worksheet

Official FAR Part 47: https://www.acquisition.gov/far/part-47

Source baseline: FAC 2026-01, effective March 13, 2026; checked November 3, 2026. Check the actual contract and applicable agency deviations.

Explore GovAssessment: https://govsuccess.com/
A structured business-readiness baseline based on your answers; no compliance certification or award guarantee.

General education, not legal or tax advice.

#GovSuccess #FAR #GovernmentContracting

00:29 Identify the transaction and delivery point
01:09 Separate freight charges from risk and acceptance
01:56 Check routing and carrier restrictions
02:15 Check the applicable framework
02:38 A hypothetical example
03:14 Avoid the shortcut
03:41 Build a contractor worksheet
04:11 Use the worksheet
04:29 Three operating checks
04:51 Build your readiness baseline

metadata.title: Neybor FAR Part12
metadata.author: Neybor Consulting
metadata.shortDescription:
FAR Part 12 establishes the rules for how the federal government buys commercial products and services—meaning items that are already sold in the marketplace. The goal is to make government buying faster, more efficient, and aligned with standard business practices rather than overly complex federal procedures.

This part allows agencies to:

* Use streamlined acquisition methods instead of heavy regulations
* Rely on market pricing and competition rather than cost-based pricing
* Incorporate commercial terms and conditions, minimizing unique government requirements
* Reduce administrative burden for both agencies and contractors

For contractors, FAR Part 12 is a major advantage. It lowers barriers to entry, shortens procurement timelines, and allows businesses to sell to the government in a way that closely mirrors how they sell commercially. However, companies must still ensure compliance with required clauses, representations, and certifications—especially those tied to labor, environmental, and socio-economic regulations.

Key takeaway: If your product or service is already sold commercially, FAR Part 12 is one of the fastest and most accessible pathways into federal contracting.

If you want to position your business to win more commercial item contracts under FAR Part 12, Neybor Consulting can help you structure your offerings, pricing strategy, and compliance approach. Reach out today to start building a government-ready commercial sales strategy.

metadata.title: BREAKING NEWS: DOJ Busts Ghost Student Fraud Ring — October 29th, 2026
metadata.author: Politics_Shmolitics
metadata.shortDescription:
On October 29, 2026, the Justice Department announced the first indictments of Operation Ghostbusters, a nationwide investigation into what officials call a large-scale student loan fraud scheme. Five defendants were charged in three federal districts — New Jersey, Nebraska, and the Eastern District of Virginia — accused of using stolen American identities to enroll so-called ghost students at colleges and divert federal student aid refunds to accounts they controlled.

Prosecutors say the scheme worked through the refund: after tuition and fees were paid, the leftover aid money meant for a real student's living expenses was sent to bank accounts held by the participants, including money mules in the United States who kept a share and wired the rest to associates in Kenya, some of it tied to a purported safari company. In New Jersey, three people were arrested on a wire fraud conspiracy complaint, with an intended loss listed at $1.5 million. In Nebraska, Francis Mogambi was indicted on theft of government money and aggravated identity theft charges. In Virginia, a sealed indictment covers more than 700 fraudulent refund deposits worth about $1.44 million.

The scale behind the five charges is what investigators keep stressing. In September and October 2026 alone, teams identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts linked to nearly $130 million and recommended the Department of Education disable them. The FBI says it has identified more than $32 million in losses, with millions more suspected, and the Justice Department estimates total losses well over $200 million since 2021, across 45 investigations, more than 40 open cases, 26 FBI field offices, and more than 20 U.S. Attorneys' offices. Investigators also seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency, which the department calls the first international seizure of its kind in Fraud Division history.

What happens next will be fought over in courtrooms and in Congress: the charged defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty, the flagged accounts must be reviewed so real students are not swept up, and colleges and agencies face pressure to tighten identity checks without making aid harder for the millions of legitimate students who depend on it. This video lays out the verified facts, the three cases, and both sides of the debate over the fix.

metadata.title: OPERATION GHOSTBUSTERS — The $200 Million Ghost Student Fraud
metadata.author: Scamverge
metadata.shortDescription:
On October 29, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the first results of Operation Ghostbusters, a nationwide investigation into alleged fraud against federal student aid. Five defendants were charged in three separate federal cases in Virginia, Nebraska, and New Jersey. Prosecutors allege that stolen American identities were used to file fraudulent FAFSA applications, enrol "ghost students" who never attended class, and divert the leftover aid refunds through U.S.-based money mules to associates in Kenya — with more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency seized. This video keeps four often-confused figures strictly separate: FBI-identified losses of more than $32 million in similar schemes; a wider-problem estimate of well over $200 million since 2021; 830,840 potentially fraudulent aid IDs flagged in September–October 2026, linked to nearly $130 million (flagged, not proven theft); and the $750,000+ seized (money recovered, not money stolen). IMPORTANT: all five defendants are charged/alleged only and are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. The Virginia case remains under seal and its defendant is unnamed in the Justice Department release — this video names nobody for that case.

CHAPTERS:
00:00 — The announcement: Operation Ghostbusters
01:10 — What is a ghost student?
02:12 — The fake classroom
03:24 — Four numbers — do not mix them
04:54 — Virginia: the sealed case
06:08 — Nebraska: Francis Mogambi
07:43 — New Jersey: the money mules
09:03 — Kenya and the $750,000 seizure
10:11 — The real victims
11:29 — What happens next

segments.text: On October 29th, 2026, the United States Justice Department announced the first results of an investigation with a name straight out of a movie: Operation Ghostbusters.
Five defendants were charged in three separate federal cases, in Virginia, Nebraska, and New Jersey.
The alleged crime was not a bank robbery, and it was not a hack of a vault.

Prosecutors say it was something quieter, and harder to see: students who did not exist, enrolled in real colleges, collecting real federal student aid, with the money diverted to bank accounts and then overseas.
Before we go any further, one thing must be clear.
These are charges, not convictions.
An indictment or a criminal complaint is only an allegation, and every defendant in this story is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in a court of law.
With that guardrail in place, here is what the Justice Department says happened, and why officials are calling this only the beginning.
So what is a ghost student? According to the Justice Department, the scheme starts with a stolen identity.

Criminal actors take the personal information of a real American citizen, often someone who has never been to college, and use it to file a fraudulent federal student aid application, known as a FAFSA.
The fake student is then enrolled at a college or university.
When federal loan and grant money arrives, the school takes its tuition and fees, and the leftover money is paid out as a refund.
In a legitimate case, that refund helps a real student pay for rent, books, or food.
In this alleged scheme, prosecutors say the refund never reached a student at all, because there was no student.
The ghost never attended class.
Instead, the money was routed to bank accounts controlled by the network, and moved on by people inside the United States acting as money mules.
To keep the ghost alive, prosecutors say the fraudsters went further.

The Justice Department describes fake students being placed in online classrooms to create the appearance that a real person was present, and automated tools being used to complete required coursework, so the aid kept flowing.
That is what makes this different from a single forged form.
It is a performance, sustained over semesters, designed to pass the checks that schools and the government use to confirm that a student is real and learning.

The department says this kind of fraud has been going on since at least 2021, and that community colleges and universities across the country first spotted fraudulent applications that resulted in refunds going to accounts opened in someone else's name.
At a news conference on October 29th, officials said that in California alone, one third of community college applications submitted in 2024 were flagged as fraudulent.
That figure is a flag rate, not a conviction count, and it shows why investigators say the problem is far bigger than five defendants.
Now, the numbers in this case need careful handling, because four different figures are circulating, and they measure four different things.
Do not add them together, and do not swap them.
First, the FBI says it has identified more than 32 million dollars in losses in similar ghost student schemes, with millions more suspected.
That is identified losses. Second, the Justice Department estimates the wider fraud problem at well over 200 million dollars since 2021.
That is an estimate of the overall problem under investigation, not a proven loss in these five cases.

Third, in September and October of 2026, investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent federal student aid IDs, linked to nearly 130 million dollars, and recommended that the Department of Education disable those IDs.
Flagged is not convicted, and associated aid is not proven theft.
Fourth, investigators seized more than 750,000 dollars in cryptocurrency connected to the scheme.
That is money recovered, not money stolen.
Keep those four apart, and the story stays honest.
The Virginia case is the one closest to home for viewers in Northern Virginia, and it comes with a limit we will respect in this video.
On October 21st, a federal grand jury in the Eastern District of Virginia returned a multi-count indictment charging a Kenyan national with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and student aid fraud.
The indictment remains under seal, and the Justice Department did not name the defendant.
We will not name anyone the release does not name.

What prosecutors allege is specific: the defendant acted as a United States based money mule, using multiple bank accounts across several financial institutions to receive more than 700 fraudulently obtained federal student aid refund deposits, totalling approximately 1,439,548 dollars.
Prosecutors say at least 1.3 million dollars was then moved through thousands of wire transfer and money service transactions to accounts in the United States and Kenya.
The intended loss in this case is listed as 1.4 million dollars.
Again, alleged, not proven.
The Nebraska case names its defendant, and it reads very differently in scale.
On October 19th, a federal grand jury indicted Francis Mogambi, a Kenyan citizen, on ten counts: five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.

Prosecutors allege that between November 2025 and May 2026, Mogambi worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of American citizens, fraudulently enrol them in educational institutions, and redirect federal financial aid cheques to himself.
The alleged split was stark: he kept 30 percent of the proceeds and sent the rest to his conspirators in Kenya.

Court documents also allege that he tried to recruit another person into the scheme, telling that person he received 2,000 dollars a week, and that he needed a business so he could cash larger cheques and avoid paying taxes.

The Justice Department lists the intended loss in the Nebraska case as 20,000 dollars, a much smaller case figure than Virginia's, and a reminder that intended loss is a charging figure for one case, not a measure of the whole network.
Mogambi arrived in the United States on May 15th, 2024, after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, according to the release.
He was arrested promptly and detained pending trial.
The third case, in New Jersey, is where the money mule role is described in the most detail.
Three defendants were arrested on a criminal complaint: Mabed Patricia Utate-Alberto, Patricia Arisleydi Perez, and George Arturo Alfau Mendez.

Prosecutors allege that from about March 2021 through at least January 2026, the three conspired with people located in Kenya to defraud the Department of Education, obtaining more than 1 million dollars in federal student aid funds through false FAFSA applications using stolen American identities.

The Justice Department describes them as witting money mules: people who knew what they were doing, receiving the money in United States bank accounts, taking their cut, and transferring the rest overseas to co-conspirators in Kenya associated with a purported Kenyan safari company.
The intended loss in the New Jersey case is listed as 1.5 million dollars.
Two co-conspirators in Kenya are associated with that safari company, and the government says it will seek to charge them as the case continues.
That Kenya connection is also where the seizure happened.
In September, representatives of the Justice Department's Fraud Division and its agency partners visited Kenya to promote extradition, prosecution, and the return of stolen assets.

With assistance and intelligence from Kenyan law enforcement partners, investigators seized more than 750,000 dollars from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the scheme.
The Justice Department calls it the first international seizure of its kind in the history of its Fraud Division.
The Kenyan partners named in the release are the Directorate of Criminal Investigations, the Asset Recovery Agency, and the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald, who leads the department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, put it bluntly: whether you are in Nebraska, New Jersey, Virginia, or Nairobi, we will pursue you.
Officials stressed that this announcement is the first round, not the final word.
Behind every figure in this story is a real person whose identity was allegedly stolen, and that is the part that deserves the most attention.
The Justice Department says many known victims had only attained a high school diploma, and were shocked to learn of fake attendance at an institution hundreds of miles away.
Imagine getting a letter, or a bill, or a tax document, for a college you never attended, in a state you may never have visited, for a loan you never took.
Some victims only learned what had happened when the FBI wrote to them.
The department's release points victims to the Department of Education's inspector general hotline, and says anyone who received an FBI letter should follow the instructions in it.
There is a second group of victims, too: real students.

Every dollar diverted to a ghost is a dollar that cannot help a real student pay for an education, and the Department of Education says it has saved taxpayers more than 2 billion dollars in attempted student aid theft.
That is the department's own claim, and it is a claim about attempts stopped, not money recovered.
So what happens next? The investigation is not closed.

The Justice Department says there are now more than 40 open cases across 26 FBI field offices and more than 20 United States Attorneys' offices, after the FBI's Richmond field office opened the investigation following a referral from the Department of Education's inspector general, and the Eastern District of Virginia sent approximately 50 referrals around the country.
More charges are expected. For ordinary people, the practical lessons are simple, and they cost nothing.
Check whether a FAFSA or a student loan exists in your name, even if you never applied.
Freeze your credit if you have not already.
Treat any unexpected student aid letter, refund cheque, or tax form as a red flag, not junk mail.
And if you believe your identity was used, report it through the Department of Education's hotline.
The ghost students were designed to be invisible.
The investigation's message is that data leaves a trail, and that trail, prosecutors say, is now being followed wherever it leads.
Until a court decides otherwise, though, remember the line this story started with: charged is not convicted, and every defendant remains presumed innocent.
