Flagged is not convicted, and associated aid is not proven theft. Fourth, investigators seized more than 750,000 dollars in cryptocurrency connected to the scheme. That is money recovered, not money stolen. Keep those four apart, and the story stays honest. The Virginia case is the one closest to home for viewers in Northern Virginia, and it comes with a limit we will respect in this video. On October 21st, a federal grand jury in the Eastern District of Virginia returned a multi-count indictment charging a Kenyan national with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and student aid fraud. The indictment remains under seal, and the Justice Department did not name the defendant. We will not name anyone the release does not name. What prosecutors allege is specific: the defendant acted as a United States based money mule, using multiple bank accounts across several financial institutions to receive more than 700 fraudulently obtained federal student aid refund deposits, totalling approximately 1,439,548 dollars. Prosecutors say at least 1.3 million dollars was then moved through thousands of wire transfer and money service transactions to accounts in the United States and Kenya. The intended loss in this case is listed as 1.4 million dollars. Again, alleged, not proven. The Nebraska case names its defendant, and it reads very differently in scale. On October 19th, a federal grand jury indicted Francis Mogambi, a Kenyan citizen, on ten counts: five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft. Prosecutors allege that between November 2025 and May 2026, Mogambi worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of American citizens, fraudulently enrol them in educational institutions, and redirect federal financial aid cheques to himself. The alleged split was stark: he kept 30 percent of the proceeds and sent the rest to his conspirators in Kenya. Court documents also allege that he tried to recruit another person into the scheme, telling that person he received 2,000 dollars a week, and that he needed a business so he could cash larger cheques and avoid paying taxes. The Justice Department lists the intended loss in the Nebraska case as 20,000 dollars, a much smaller case figure than Virginia's, and a reminder that intended loss is a charging figure for one case, not a measure of the whole network. Mogambi arrived in the United States on May 15th, 2024, after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, according to the release. He was arrested promptly and detained pending trial. The third case, in New Jersey, is where the money mule role is described in the most detail. Three defendants were arrested on a criminal complaint: Mabed Patricia Utate-Alberto, Patricia Arisleydi Perez, and George Arturo Alfau Mendez. Prosecutors allege that from about March 2021 through at least January 2026, the three conspired with people located in Kenya to defraud the Department of Education, obtaining more than 1 million dollars in federal student aid funds through false FAFSA applications using stolen American identities. The Justice Department describes them as witting money mules: people who knew what they were doing, receiving the money in United States bank accounts, taking their cut, and transferring the rest overseas to co-conspirators in Kenya associated with a purported Kenyan safari company. The intended loss in the New Jersey case is listed as 1.5 million dollars. Two co-conspirators in Kenya are associated with that safari company, and the government says it will seek to charge them as the case continues. That Kenya connection is also where the seizure happened. In September, representatives of the Justice Department's Fraud Division and its agency partners visited Kenya to promote extradition, prosecution, and the return of stolen assets. With assistance and intelligence from Kenyan law enforcement partners, investigators seized more than 750,000 dollars from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the scheme. The Justice Department calls it the first international seizure of its kind in the history of its Fraud Division. The Kenyan partners named in the release are the Directorate of Criminal Investigations, the Asset Recovery Agency, and the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald, who leads the department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, put it bluntly: whether you are in Nebraska, New Jersey, Virginia, or Nairobi, we will pursue you. Officials stressed that this announcement is the first round, not the final word. Behind every figure in this story is a real person whose identity was allegedly stolen, and that is the part that deserves the most attention. The Justice Department says many known victims had only attained a high school diploma, and were shocked to learn of fake attendance at an institution hundreds of miles away. Imagine getting a letter, or a bill, or a tax document, for a college you never attended, in a state you may never have visited, for a loan you never took. Some victims only learned what had happened when the FBI wrote to them. The department's release points victims to the Department of Education's inspector general hotline, and says anyone who received an FBI letter should follow the instructions in it. There is a second group of victims, too: real students. Every dollar diverted to a ghost is a dollar that cannot help a real student pay for an education, and the Department of Education says it has saved taxpayers more than 2 billion dollars in attempted student aid theft. That is the department's own claim, and it is a claim about attempts stopped, not money recovered. So what happens next? The investigation is not closed. The Justice Department says there are now more than 40 open cases across 26 FBI field offices and more than 20 United States Attorneys' offices, after the FBI's Richmond field office opened the investigation following a referral from the Department of Education's inspector general, and the Eastern District of Virginia sent approximately 50 referrals around the country. More charges are expected. For ordinary people, the practical lessons are simple, and they cost nothing. Check whether a FAFSA or a student loan exists in your name, even if you never applied. Freeze your credit if you have not already. Treat any unexpected student aid letter, refund cheque, or tax form as a red flag, not junk mail. And if you believe your identity was used, report it through the Department of Education's hotline. The ghost students were designed to be invisible. The investigation's message is that data leaves a trail, and that trail, prosecutors say, is now being followed wherever it leads. Until a court decides otherwise, though, remember the line this story started with: charged is not convicted, and every defendant remains presumed innocent.

metadata.title: Operation Ghostbusters: 5 Charged in the 'Ghost Student' Financial Aid Fraud
metadata.author: Court Files
metadata.shortDescription:
Five people charged. More than 830,000 potentially fraudulent student aid accounts flagged. And a fraud prosecutors say is worth well over $200 million — built on students who do not exist.

On October 29, 2026, the Justice Department announced the first charges in Operation Ghostbusters, a nationwide investigation into "ghost student" fraud: criminals who allegedly steal Americans' identities, file federal student aid applications in their names, enrol the phantom students in real colleges, and divert the refund money overseas. Artificial intelligence, prosecutors say, completes the coursework and fakes classroom attendance to keep the money flowing. Three weeks later, the FBI said the investigation is escalating — 47 separate investigations, in nearly half of the Bureau's field offices.

This is the full story — the victim who found a $10,000 loan in his name, the three cases in New Jersey, Virginia and Nebraska, the Kenya connection and the $750,000 cryptocurrency seizure, and what happens next.

**Chapters**
0:00 Cold Open — "We Will Pursue You"
0:31 The Victim
1:54 How the Scam Works
3:54 Three Cases
6:58 The Kenya Connection
8:07 The Scale
9:48 November 18: The Escalation
10:56 Where It Stands

**Sources**
- U.S. Department of Justice, press release 26-1278: "Justice Department Unveils Indictments in Nationwide 'Ghost Student' Fraud Scam Linked to Kenyan Network," October 29, 2026 — https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-unveils-indictments-nationwide-ghost-student-fraud-scam-linked-kenyan
- U.S. Department of Justice press conference, October 29, 2026 (The Justice Department, YouTube) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=go_UzlnlFDE
- ABC News: "'It's appalling': Feds ramp up investigations of 'ghost student' fraud," November 18, 2026 (ABC Audio mirror) — https://otterrockradio.com/2026/11/18/its-appalling-feds-ramp-up-investigations-of-ghost-student-fraud/
- USA Today: "'Operation Ghostbusters': DOJ unveils crackdown on student aid fraud scheme," October 29, 2026 — https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2026/10/29/ghost-busters-federal-student-aid-fraud-scheme/92496539007/

**Attribution:** the account of the scheme — the stolen identities, the fraudulent FAFSA applications, the diverted refunds, the money mules, the safari-company connection, and the dollar figures for each case — comes from the Justice Department's October 29, 2026 press release and the charging documents it describes. The figure of 830,840 potentially fraudulent student aid IDs is a count of flagged accounts, not confirmed fake students; the nearly $130 million tied to them is a conditional estimate. The "well over $200 million" figure is the Justice Department's estimate of the fraud's scale since at least 2021, not a confirmed loss total. The FBI's confirmed loss figure is more than $32 million. The account of Tony Rice, of Mogambi's roommate turning him in, and of the 47 investigations comes from ABC News, November 18, 2026. The claim that the Department of Education saved taxpayers more than $2 billion in attempted student aid theft is the Department's own statement and is not repeated in this video.

**Presumption of innocence:** an indictment, information, or complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Francis Mogambi has pleaded not guilty. The Virginia defendant has not been named; the indictment remains under seal.

**Fair use notice:** this video uses brief excerpts (each under 4 seconds) of copyrighted news broadcasts for the purpose of news reporting and commentary, with transformative editing. The press-conference footage is a U.S. government work (U.S. Department of Justice) and is in the public domain. All rights in news material belong to their owners.

**Stock footage:** some images are illustrative stock footage and do not show the people, places or property in this case.

Every case. From the official record.
Subscribe for the next one — we follow every case we cover.

metadata.author: Dr. Wes Fisher
metadata.shortDescription:
How To Win A Government Contract In 5 Days (2025) | Step-by-Step Guide

Are you ready to win your first government contract but keep getting stuck? If you have a CAGE code and you’re registered on SAM.gov, but you haven’t submitted a proposal yet, this video is for you!

In this guide, I’m going to break down exactly how you can go from zero to submitted in just 5 days—even if you’ve never bid on a contract before. This is a proven system that has helped my students win millions in federal contracts, and if you follow these steps, you’ll be on your way to landing your first contract fast.

Here’s What You’ll Learn:
✔️ Step 1: How to find the right opportunities on SAM.gov

metadata.title: Project Bid-Desk - Proposal
metadata.author: Estimight
metadata.shortDescription:
Create stunning, professional client bid proposals and win more construction contracts with this complete guide to the Proposals Tab in Estimight. Learn how to transform your estimate into a polished client-facing document, customize pricing breakdown visibility, add optional upgrades and deductions, structure milestone payment schedules, attach takeoff drawings, and automate branding templates.

Start streamlining your construction bids and proposals at https://estimight.com

What You’ll Learn in This Video:
Estimate-to-Proposal Sync: Automatically generate detailed, client-ready proposals directly from your priced estimate with instant price refresh.

Granular Pricing Table Controls: Choose exactly what your client sees—show or hide unit costs, itemized quantities, markups, or lump-sum category totals.

Direct Page Editing & Custom Styling: Edit introductory copy and terms directly on the page, set custom banner headers, fonts, colors, and layout alignments.

Adding Client Options & Variations: Include opt-in add-ons (e.g., stone benchtop upgrade) or deductions (e.g., owner-supplied tiles) outside the base contract total.

Custom Sections & Reordering: Add inclusions, exclusions, bullet lists, terms and conditions, and drag sections to reorder page flow.

Milestone Payment Schedules: Set deposit, frame stage, lockup, and completion percentages with automatic dollar calculations and validation.

Drawings & Markup Appendix: Attach marked-up takeoff drawings, selected plan sheets, or clean PDFs directly into the proposal appendix.

Professional Cover Pages & Branding: Upload cover imagery and company logos, configure license/ABN details, set validity periods, and customize page footers.

Proposal Templates & Revisions: Save proposal designs as reusable company templates, freeze sent revisions, track bid history, and export high-resolution PDFs.

Timestamps:
0:00 – Introduction: Proposals Overview & Estimate Sync

0:25 – Live Document Preview & Page Break Indicators

0:51 – Pricing Table Controls: Unit Rates vs. Lump Sum

1:22 – Customizing Headings, Fonts & Inline Text Editing

1:54 – Client Options: Adding Upgrades & Deductions

2:40 – Managing Sections: Inclusions, Exclusions & Reordering

3:33 – Building a Milestone Payment Schedule

4:19 – Drawings Appendix: Attaching Takeoff Sheets & Markups

4:46 – Designing a Custom Cover Page

5:17 – Document Design: Titles, Alignment & Global Styles

6:00 – Letterhead, Company Branding & License Details

6:31 – Theme Colors, Typography & Page Footers

7:00 – Saving & Applying Reusable Proposal Templates

7:27 – Revision History, Refreshing Prices & PDF Export

7:42 – Sending Proposals, Freezing Revisions & Next Steps

About Estimight
Estimight is modern construction estimating and bid management software built to help contractors, builders, and estimators streamline takeoffs, build accurate estimates, and deliver winning client proposals.

Website: https://estimight.com

Subscribe: Subscribe to our channel for more construction estimating tutorials, bid management tips, and takeoff workflows.

#Estimight #ConstructionProposals #BidProposal #ConstructionEstimating #ContractorSoftware #ConstructionSoftware #BidManagement #ClientProposals

metadata.title: Janitorial Government Contracts Up 25% | 5 SLED Bids to Watch | TWIP Ep. 42
metadata.author: Government Contracting Strategist & Host
metadata.shortDescription:
Looking for janitorial government contracts to bid on this week?

Janitorial opportunities on state, local, and education bid boards jumped 25% in one week.

And that matters because cleaning is not one-time work.

Buildings reopen.
Buses run again tomorrow.
Rest areas stay open.
Games happen every week.

That means janitorial contracts can become some of the most consistent recurring work in government contracting.

In Episode 42 of This Week in Procurement, Abby Souffrant breaks down 5 current SLED cleaning contracts and the pipeline lessons behind them.

🧹 5 Janitorial Government Contracts This Week

🚏 Everett, Washington — Transit Stops & Park-and-Ride Cleaning

Cleaning across 600+ service points, including bus stops, shelters, and park-and-ride locations.

Pipeline lesson: Route-based contracts should not always be priced like buildings. Track stops, frequency, travel time, labor hours, and service density.

🚌 Miami, Florida — Bus Cleaning & Disinfecting

Nightly detail cleaning and disinfecting for an expanding transit fleet.

Pipeline lesson: Fleet growth can signal future contract growth. Do not just price today’s bus count—understand how the agency expects the fleet to change.

🚻 Craven County, North Carolina — Highway Rest Area Custodial Services

Custodial operations and maintenance for a US-70 rest area along the future Interstate 42 corridor.

Pipeline lesson: Infrastructure growth creates recurring service demand. When roads expand, support contracts often expand with them.

🏢 Boulder, Colorado — Citywide Custodial Services

Custodial work across multiple city facilities as Boulder reshapes its facility footprint.

Pipeline lesson: Facility changes can create contract changes. Track square footage, building closures, new locations, and service frequency before you finalize pricing.

🏟️ Starkville, Mississippi — Athletic Facility & Game-Day Cleaning

Cleaning support for Mississippi State University Athletics, including both daily facility maintenance and event surges.

Pipeline lesson: Event cleaning is not the same as routine custodial work. Your pricing has to account for labor spikes, turnaround windows, and unpredictable volume.

💡 This Week’s Strategy: Square Feet vs. Service Points

A lot of cleaning companies default to:

“What’s the square footage?”

But that is not always the best pricing model.

For route-based, fleet-based, and event-driven contracts, the better question may be:

How many service points am I responsible for?

That could mean:

✅ Stops
✅ Buses
✅ Restrooms
✅ Buildings
✅ Events
✅ Game days

The wrong pricing unit can destroy your margin before the contract even starts.

So do not just price the space.

Price the workload.

📩 Want daily state, local, and education government contracting insights?

Subscribe to the SLED Executive Briefing for a quick daily look at procurement activity across the country.

🔗 Link pinned in the comments.

👇 If you own a cleaning company, which would you rather bid on: buildings, buses, or events?
